title: RG Snyman in advanced talks with TOP14 club
article_text:
Stade Français are in advanced talks with Leinster lock RG Snyman about ending his seven-year stay in Ireland and moving to the Top 14 to solve one of their problem areas next season.

Leinster bosses have turned to Snyman, 31, who has helped the Springboks win back-to-back World Cup crowns, after missing out on Australian-born French international Emmanuel Meafou.

Stade made a big play for Meafou to add strength to an area that has been lacking since Baptiste Pesenti, who has four Les Bleus caps, departed in the summer for Pau, but he has decided to stay in Toulouse until 2032.

Snyman, who was voted United Rugby Championship player of the year in 2025, joined Munster seven years ago after a stint in Japan with Tochigi Honda Heat and is in his third year with Leinster but is yet to play a game this season.

His move to Dublin was controversial. He had been set to reunite with Johann van Graan at Bath, only to end up signing for Leinster, where he has made over 30 appearances before rupturing knee ligaments against Glasgow Warriors in March.

Stade have been speaking to Snyman, who appears to be very open to a move to the French capital when his contract runs out at the end of the season, and they have been edging closer to agreeing a deal in the last few days.

And he could become the second massive name to arrive at the Stade Jean-Bouin in a matter of days after it was revealed that All Black star Wallace Sititi is expected to swap the Chiefs for Les Soldats Roses late next year after the World Cup in Australia.

Sititi, 24, is expected to sign a two-year deal with Stade, who, after qualifying for the Top 14 play-offs last season, have found this campaign much harder, sitting in ninth place with 19 points from their nine games.

title: France boss responds to Springboks and All Blacks doping controversy
article_text:
France head coach Fabien Galthie has expressed his surprise after reports revealed that no random post-match drug tests were carried out during the entire Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry tour between South Africa and New Zealand.

An investigation by The Times found that none of the eight matches on the tour, which included four provincial fixtures and four Tests, featured random post-match drug testing.

Almost 170 players took part across the series, with New Zealand Rugby confirming that none of its players were tested during the trip.

The South African Institute for Drug-Free Sport (SAIDS), which oversees the testing programme, said its priority was out-of-competition testing.

It insisted that no regulations had been broken, while World Rugby defended its wider anti-doping programme.

The number of tests has fallen by around 70 per cent over the past decade, dropping from 753 in 2015/16 to just 225 in 2025/26.

The revelations come just days before the Springboks face France in the inaugural Nations Championship final. There is, however, no suggestion of wrongdoing by either team during the tour.

Galthie has now given his reaction to the findings, speaking to RMC Sport about the importance of regular testing and fairness in the game.

"This is something very important. Very, very important. In any case, we are very sensitive to it. To the health of the players and to fairness.

"We have been tested three times since November, three times in Marcoussis, three times at 6:30 am, three times four players. We participate very attentively in the tests imposed on us by World Rugby."

The France boss admitted he was particularly surprised by the suggestion that some teams had not been tested throughout the tour.

"I am surprised, very surprised by what you are telling me this morning, that some teams have not been tested. I don't know if it's fair, if it's true. But in any case, we are paying close attention to it. Testing, fairness, it's very important in our sport.

"This is the governing body of world rugby. So the reins belong to World Rugby. Since it's their competition, it's World Rugby that organises fairness and equity within its competition.

"World Rugby is responsible for fairness. I don't know if the information is accurate, but for me it's crucial and very important. We pay close attention to it. We like and want to be audited regularly."

title: How to qualify for rugby sevens at LA28: The qualification system explained
Dubai 7s Invitational: What to expect from the five competing teams
article_text:
The International Invitation competition is the highest rank of the competition outside of the SVNS circuit.

In past years, it’s been a heavily stacked competition, with national sides getting in some reps ahead of the season and charity assembly teams testing their mettle against the best.

This year’s competition looks a little different. The 2025 competition had two pools of five, producing a leaderboard that went on to a knockout finals stage at the iconic Dubai 7s stadium.

This year, with the introduction of the SVNS 3, many of those International Invitational sides have moved into the expanded SVNS set-up. But the Invitational remains high quality.

Ireland, Brazil, Belgium and Hammerheads all return this year to the International Invitational, with 7s up-and-comers Germany looking to make an impact too.

Hammerheads are the last assembly team standing. A privately run, sponsorship-backed team by Leiden Contractors, born from Head Coach Jim Osborne, Hammerheads are an iconic staple of the UK 7s circuit turned international touring team.

In a landscape where opportunities for female players to gain top-level minutes outside of international training camps are still frighteningly small, Hammerheads are bringing a stacked team of international talent to this Dubai 7s.

The squad almost mirrors an Ultimate 7s team, hosting players of eight nationalities including USA flyer Nia Toliver and GB sevens stalwart Isla Norman-Bell, as well as New Zealand up-and-comer Manawa Rogers.

Speaking to Jim Osborne on the eve of the tournament, he reflected on entering this year’s comp as the only non-International side. He said, “It’s so hard because we’ve come out here and half of the people have never met each other, and we’ve just had to go and bond.

“We’ve got two training sessions, one today and one tomorrow, which are basically team runs. We trained at the water park today, doing set pieces, so saving a bit of time so that we don’t have to do that at the next training session.

“We started as a men’s team and brought in the women’s, but the women’s is actually what’s given us our name. Our bread and butter is the women’s side. We get messages all the time from people who want to play, and it’s just an amazing pathway for people to take the next step.

“Ireland will be the biggest challenge. And then Brazil. And then you never know what you’re going to get with Germany and Belgium.

“My dream was to win the Open, which we did four or five years ago. And so it moved from winning the Open to the fairytale ending of winning the Elite.

“Our first game is on pitch 1 against Ireland. It’s going to be unreal.”

Germany are fast becoming one of the most promising sides on the sevens circuit. In front of a strong home crowd at Hamburg at the Europeans in July, they managed a best-place finish at 4th, losing to Spain in the bronze playoff.

They take a strong squad, with no new faces on the teamsheet from their last 7s outing at Split. Mette Zimmat, Paula Schult, and Charlotte Malaizier all featured in Ultimate 7s, with Germany head coach Curtis Bradford gaining some reps too, now bound for the desert this weekend.

They always look like the team to beat. Whether they succeed in those performances against a class of competition will be the biggest test for them.

Belgium have been the underdogs of the European Sevens circuit. They earned a bronze at the European 7s Championship in July in Hamburg, and since their programme went full-time, they’ve developed in style and confidence and look organised.

Their squad for Dubai remains largely unchanged from the summer European Championships.

Lisa Goosens, Romaine Yserbyt, and Lili-Rose Scoriel all return, as well as Abigael Bokonda, who scored the bronze-winning try in Hamburg.

Violette Vekemans, Louka Blommaert and Lea Poucet are new faces in the squad for Dubai. Head coach Terry Bouhraoua will want to gain wins against fellow European teams Belgium, Germany and Ireland.

Known as the ‘Yaras’, they are the only non-European international side in this year’s competition.

Playing in SVNS 2, they’ll be a tough team to beat, bringing an experienced squad. Thalia Costa ran out for Sol Feroz in Ultimate 7s, whilst Isadora Lopes and Gabriela Lima helped bag Pacific Current the inaugural title, Lima scoring a try in the final, not only putting herself but the Brazilian rugby firmly on the map.

They are experienced, and they will be well drilled, confident and, best of all, exciting to watch.

And lastly, Ireland are taking an unbelievably stacked side this tournament. Six Nations fans will recognise members of the ‘Green Wave’ Anna McGann, Stacey Flood, and Eve Higgins, but there is pace across the board as sevens flyers Alana McInerney, Emily Lane and Kathy Baker bolster the squad. Twenty-year-old Leah Irwin earns a call-up after rising through the Ireland U21 programme with strong performances in Ulster and Enniskillen this season.

Having won the second leg of the European Sevens Championship in Split in July, where they beat Poland 26-12, they surely enter the competition as the heavily tipped favourites.

title: Jenkins ready to resume Wales captaincy role
article_text:
Dafydd Jenkins says he feels more ready now to be Wales captain, having been given the honour of leading his country again in the Nations Championship finale against Japan on Saturday.

Regular captain Dewi Lake and deputy Jac Morgan have both dropped down to the bench for the match at Allianz Stadium in Twickenham, as head coach Steve Tandy rotates his side for the-ninth place play-off.

It leaves Exeter lock Jenkins, who turns 24 next month, as the natural choice to reclaim the armband - more than two years after he was given a baptism of fire as Warren Gatland's skipper for the 2024 Six Nations.

With Lake and Morgan injured for that tournament - and a number of senior players having retired after the 2023 World Cup - Jenkins endured a tough test, as Wales suffered a clean sweep of Six Nations defeats for the first time since 2003.

"I am definitely a different person," said Jenkins, who at 21 was the second-youngest Wales captain behind Sir Gareth Edwards.

"I was looking back at when I got it the first time, I feel a lot more settled now within the squad.

"To have that experience before puts me in good stead now."

Jenkins will - for now - retake the role for just one match, with Lake and Morgan having led Wales for the past two years.

However, the 6ft 7in (2.01m) Exeter lock has always been a natural leader, claiming the record as the youngest captain in the English Prem at just 19 years and 342 days old in November 2022.

He has followed that up by becoming the Chiefs' permanent skipper for the past few seasons.

"I'm always trying to develop my game and leadership skills," said Jenkins.

"I'm probably not the loudest leader, but I try to lead through my actions and hope boys follow me.

"I love doing it at Exeter, I love putting the jersey on here with Wales, so whatever's best for the team.

"It will be another special occasion for me and my family."

Tandy says that as part of his squad's leadership group, Jenkins was the natural choice to captain the side on Saturday.

"It's massive credit for him, so well-deserved and a great opportunity for him to lead the team," said the Wales head coach.

Jenkins, Morgan and Lake make up that Wales leadership group, along with others including hooker Ryan Elias, wing Josh Adams and scrum-half Tomos Williams.

"I can't take away from the players I have around me and it is a privileged situation as a captain," added Jenkins.

"I'm very lucky to be in a situation where you have people like Josh on the wing, Ryan in the pack and Adam Beard calling line-outs."

Jenkins, who is set to be one of seven Wales players to start all four games this November, has produced a colossal defensive shift across the campaign.

His most effective contribution was the 38 tackles he made in the victory against New Zealand, during a game in which Wales made a team record of 346.

Jenkins' personal tally equalled the men's individual Test record set by France flanker Thierry Dusautoir against New Zealand in the 2007 World Cup quarter-final in Cardiff.

After missing the first half of World Rugby's new competition during the summer through injury, Jenkins has made 77 Nations Championship tackles, the most of any player, without missing one.

When asked about the tackling records, he says it is just part of his job.

"That's exactly it," said Jenkins. "If someone runs into you, you're going to make the tackle.

"If you look at [prop] Gareth Thomas, he's come off the bench [against New Zealand] and made a stupid amount of tackles, 19 in 26 minutes.

"That is ridiculous and if he's on the whole game, he'd probably double mine!

"It was a huge defensive shift from all the boys after we had been clinical in that first half.

"That's something we probably lacked [in the following week's defeat] against Australia, so we are looking to get that back now against Japan."

"I just love Daf's energy," said the former British and Irish Lions defence coach.

"The work he does in the week is phenomenal and he is the ultimate professional.

"There's a lot of skill to his game also, while the power of his mindset is one of the best I've seen.

"You look at the performance he produced against New Zealand, but he found it to go again against Australia. He made a couple of cover tackles against the Wallabies that probably saved us."

Jenkins is hoping Wales can finish off a successful November by making it three victories in four matches.

"It has been one of the most enjoyable campaigns I've been a part of," he said.

"Obviously because we beat the All Blacks, but the group is as tight as it's ever been since I've been here.

"The competition's there, the training standards are a lot higher than previously, so that's a huge positive to grow for the future."

title: Tommaso Menoncello could miss Six Nations after latest injury setback
article_text:
Italy centre Tommaso Menoncello is facing a race against time to be fit for the 2027 Six Nations after suffering another setback in his ongoing shoulder injury.

The 24-year-old initially injured his left shoulder against Exeter in October and spent five weeks on the sidelines. However, after returning to training on Monday, the problem flared up again.

Menoncello is now expected to undergo surgery next week, which could keep him out for three to four months.

The setback is a major blow for Italy, with the 41-cap centre now likely to miss the 2027 Six Nations. He had already been ruled out of the Nations Championship.

Menoncello joined French giants Toulouse ahead of the 2026/27 campaign following six years at Benetton.

He made his international debut against France in the 2022 Six Nations, scoring a try to become the youngest player to score in the tournament's history at just 19.

Since then, he has developed into one of Italy's most important players, earning the 2024 Six Nations Player of the Championship award.

His absence will be another concern for Gonzalo Quesada, whose side face Fiji at Allianz Stadium this afternoon in their final Nations Championship fixture.

Italy have collected just two points from their six summer and autumn matches, despite enjoying an encouraging Six Nations campaign earlier this year. They will be desperate to secure a first-ever victory over Fiji.

Injuries have played a significant part in their difficult run of results. Quesada was without 16 players for Italy's opening autumn fixture against South Africa, with Menoncello among those unavailable.

While the results have been disappointing, the sheer number of absentees has made life particularly difficult for the Italian head coach.

There is also a longer-term concern for Menoncello, with the timing of his recovery potentially affecting his preparations for next year's World Cup.

If he misses the Six Nations, he could go more than a year without playing Test rugby. His last appearance for Italy came against the All Blacks in July.

title: Scotland make 11 changes for Argentina game
article_text:
Scotland head coach Gregor Townsend has made 11 changes to his starting XV for Sunday's Nations Championship closer against Argentina at Twickenham (13:10 GMT).

Only record try-scoring wing Darcy Graham, centre Rory Hutchinson, scrum-half Jamie Dobie and lock Jonny Gray retain their places from last weekend's comprehensive victory against Japan, with Finn Russell back at fly-half and flanker Rory Darge returning from injury and captaining the side.

Blair Kinghorn, Kyle Steyn, Huw Jones and Darcy Graham return to the back line.

Rory Sutherland, Ewan Ashman and D'arcy Rae make up a new front row, Gregor Brown joins Gray in the second row and Josh Bayliss and Magnus Bradbury complete the back row with Darge.

"There's an opportunity with number eights out of our squad with injury," Townsend said.

"Magnus played well in the summer off the bench and he's trained well. He's come [into the squad] in good condition. I'm sure he knows it's a big opportunity for him ahead of the Six Nations.

"We feel this [centre] combination is similar to Sione [Tuipulotu] and Huw [Jones] in terms of the ball-player and the running lines of Huw outside.

"Rory hasn't had a huge amount of opportunities to play at 12 with Sione playing so many games, so it's great for him and for us to see how he goes there."

Townsend also revealed he considered playing replacement hooker Seb Stephen at number eight for this game.

"We spoke to Glasgow a few weeks ago," Townsend explained. "He came off the bench in the back row in Glasgow's last game.

"We don't think it's right this weekend, but given the quality of our three hookers, Seb probably fits that profile more than the other two. His big strength is his ball carrying. He's obviously a very good hooker, but when we're looking at potential options for the back row, he fits that profile."

The Scots and the Pumas are competing to finish seventh in the tournament.

Townsend's Scotland have won four and lost twice so far, while Felipe Contepomi's Argentina have won twice and lost on four occasions.

Contepomi makes three personnel changes with Rodrigo Isgro taking over from Bautista Delguy on the wing and Faustino Sanchez Valarolo coming in at inside centre for Justo Piccardo, who makes the bench.

Juan Martin Scelzo moves from seven to eight with Joaquin Moro coming in at openside and Facundo Isa dropping out.

"They have changed how they've defended over the last few games," Townsend added.

"They are much more aggressive with their line speed, hitting hard and looking to put bodies into contact. With that, there are threats and opportunities.

"They have always had a really good forward pack and they've got talented, skilful backs. We're expecting a top performance from them."

Scotland: Blair Kinghorn, Kyle Steyn, Huw Jones, Rory Hutchinson, Darcy Graham, Finn Russell, Jamie Dobie; Rory Sutherland, Ewan Ashman, D'arcy Rae, Gregor Brown, Jonny Gray, Josh Bayliss, Rory Darge (capt), Magnus Bradbury.

Replacements: Seb Stephen, Nathan McBeth, Zander Fagerson, Max Williamson, Liam McConnell, Ollie Leatherbarrow, George Horne, Tom Jordan.

Argentina: Geronimo Prisciantelli, Rodrigo Isgro, Lucio Cinti, Faustino Sanchez Valarolo, Ignacio Mendy, Tomas Albornoz, Gonzalo Garcia; Rodrigo Martinez, Julian Montoya (capt), Francisco Moreno, Guido Petti, Pedro Rubiolo, Juan Martin Gonzalez, Joaquin Moro, Juan Martin Scelzo.

Replacements: Facundo Bosch, Joel Sclavi, Tomas Rapetti, Efrain Elias, Santiago Grondona, Agustin Moyano, Justo Piccardo, Tobias Wade.

title: France team: Galthié responds to Rassie's ploy while sharpshooter Ramos returns for Springboks rematch
article_text:
France have been bolstered by key returnees for the grudge Nations Championship final rematch against the Springboks on Sunday at Allianz Stadium, Twickenham.

Fabien Galthié has recalled sharpshooter full-back Thomas Ramos for the final with the Toulouse star recovering from injury and having subsequently been recalled for a first cap this month.

He lines up in the number 15 jersey with Théo Attissogbe shifting to the wing while World Rugby Player of the Year nominee Louis Bielle-Biarrey rounds out the back-three.

Attissogbe replaces Aaron Grandidier-Nkanang, who has been ruled out through injury after some impressive performances this year earned him a nomination for the World Rugby Breakthrough Player of the Year Award.

The centres remain unchanged yet again with Yoram Moefana combining with Kalvin Gourgues – a combination that has gone untouched throughout November.

Meanwhile, Les Bleus have been further boosted by Matthieu Jalibert’s return at fly-half with the Bordeaux pivot getting his second start this month after returning from his spell on the sidelines last weekend against Argentina. When France last faced the Boks, they were contending with an injury crisis in the number 10 position with captain Antoine Dupont filling the void but Jalibert has eased those woes as he partners the skipper in the halfbacks.

Into the pack and Anthony Jelonch will combine with Cameron Woki and Francois Cros, the latter duo reclaiming their starting roles after being rested against Argentina while the former replaces Gregory Alldritt from the teamsheet that beat South Africa a fortnight ago.

Florian Verhaeghe and Mickaël Guillard are the starting locks for the French while hooker Maxime Lamothe is flanked by tighthead Sipili Falatea and loosehead Jefferson Poirot in the front-row.

Galthié has opted for a 6-2 bench split for the final with Peato Mauvaka named as the replacement hooker, along with props Jean-Baptiste Gros and Régis Montagne. Gros was a doubt throughout the week but has recovered in time to feature on the bench, with Galthié perhaps replying to Rassie Erasmus’ decision to name his strongest scrummaging front-row on the bench too.

Charles Ollivon and Tyler Duguid provide back-row and lock cover along with Oscar Jégou, who also makes a timely return from injury to feature in the team while Maxime Lucu and Emilien Gailleton are named as the replacement backs.

title: Thomas Ramos returns for France in Nations Championship final against Springboks
article_text:
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

France have been boosted by the return of Thomas Ramos as they battle South Africa in the inaugural Nations Championship final.

Ramos has not featured for his country since kicking a match-winning penalty against England in the Six Nations, but is passed fit to feature at Twickenham’s Allianz Stadium.

Matthieu Jalibert continues at fly half with Antoine Dupont wearing No 9, while Jefferson Poirot starts in an all-Bordeaux Begles front row.

Six forwards are held in reserve on the bench, with Maxime Lucu and Emilien Gailleton providing backline cover.

France pipped the Springboks 21-19 in an epic encounter at the Stade de France a fortnight ago, and have also beaten Fiji and Argentina this November.

France XV: 1 Jefferson Poirot, 2 Maxime Lamothe, 3 Sipili Falatea; 4 Florian Verhaege, 5 Mickael Guillard; 6 Francois Cros, 7 Cameron Woki, 8 Anthony Jelonch; 9 Antoine Dupont (capt.), 10 Matthieu Jalibert; 11 Louis Bielle-Biarrey, 12 Yoram Moefana, 13 Kalvin Gourgues, 14 Theo Attissogbe; 15 Thomas Ramos.

Replacements: 16 Peato Mauvaka, 17 Jean-Baptiste Gros, 18 Regis Montagne, 19 Charles Ollivon, 20 Tyler Duguid, 21 Oscar Jegou; 22 Maxime Lucu, 23 Emilien Gailleton.

title: Twickenham set to be half empty for Nations Championship finals opening night
article_text:
The start of the Nations Championship finals weekend will play out in front of thousands of empty seats on Friday with Twickenham's Allianz Stadium set to be filled to about half its 82,000-seater capacity.

The uppermost tier of the stadium is entirely closed, while just over half of the middle tier is open.

Tickets are on sale closer to the action, with a large proportion of seats in some lower-tier sections, notably in the north-west corner of the stadium, remaining.

The finals weekend is the climax of a new format, which repackages July and November Test fixtures and culminates in six play-off fixtures between northern and southern hemisphere sides over three days.

Friday's double-header fixture begins with Italy and Fiji, the two lowest-ranked nations, playing at 16:40 GMT, before Ireland and Australia meet in the fifth/sixth place play-off at 20:10 GMT.

Sales for Saturday and Sunday's action, which are headlined by England v New Zealand and a South Africa v France grand final respectively, are stronger.

Around 65,000 tickets have so far been bought for each, with momentum fuelled by England's five-game winning streak and France's dramatic win over the Springboks in Paris a fortnight ago.

With the identity of the teams contesting each play-off game only confirmed last weekend however, organisers have been up against time to market fixtures to the public.

Diary and budget constraints in the run-up to Christmas and the fact Allianz Stadium has already hosted capacity crowds for England's victories over Australia, Japan and New Zealand over the previous three weekends have added to the challenge.

A limited amount of 'follow my team' tickets, which allowed fans to buy further in advance and guarantee they would see a specific team over the finals weekend, were made available.

However, they came at a premium, costing more than £150. Adult tickets are available for tonight's action for £60. Even in the best remaining seats, children's prices are £20.

The sheer size of Allianz Stadium, which is behind only Wembley in terms of capacity in the United Kingdom, is also a factor.

A crowd of 22,734 came close to filling the Bluenergy Stadium to watch Fiji beat Italy in Udine last weekend. Had Ireland's match against Australia been staged at Dublin's Aviva Stadium, a 51,700 attendance would be the maximum possible.

Most of the seats on sale in the middle tier are opposite the gantry from which television cameras capture the main match action, in an apparent attempt to improve the spectacle for viewers at home.

A debrief will be carried out by the Nations Championship organisers – a new, dedicated team made up of staff from Six Nations and Sanzaar unions – before cities are given the chance to bid to host the next tournament in 2028.

Qatar had initially been slated as a potential host for that edition, but instability in the Middle East has made a return to Europe more likely.

Rugby Football Union chief executive Bill Sweeney said earlier this month that Twickenham could stage the event again, while also name-checking France and Spain, which is ambitious to prove itself as a host having bid for the 2035 Rugby World Cup, as other possible destinations.

Organisers are believed to be open-minded about changes to the staging of a competition still in its infancy.

The possibility of one city hosting the event across several stadiums, with lower-profile matches played in smaller venues is one of the developments being considered.

title: Rassie Erasmus six-match ban takes unexpected twist
article_text:
Rassie Erasmus looks increasingly likely to serve his six-match suspension in full after a surprising revelation emerged ahead of Sunday's Nations Championship final.

SA Rugby immediately announced its intention to challenge the punishment handed down by World Rugby earlier this month.

However, despite initially pushing for an expedited hearing, reports suggest the governing body never formally submitted its request.

With the Springboks preparing to face France at Twickenham, RUCK looks at how the disciplinary saga has unfolded.

South Africa suffered a 21-19 defeat to France in the Nations Championship, with several refereeing decisions becoming major talking points following the final whistle.

Speaking at a press conference in Dublin, Erasmus questioned why several incidents of suspected foul play against his players had gone unpunished.

His comments about potential match manipulation attracted the attention of World Rugby.

World Rugby announced that Erasmus had been suspended for six international matches with immediate effect.

The Springboks boss became one of three international rugby coaches banned in the space of just eight days as the governing body continued its crackdown on the mistreatment of match officials.

Erasmus retained the right to request a full misconduct hearing.

Just 20 minutes after the suspension was announced, SA Rugby released a statement signalling its intention to challenge the punishment.

The union wanted Erasmus to explain the context of his remarks and hoped a hearing could be arranged quickly.

With the Ireland Test fast approaching, Erasmus remained suspended.

The Springboks boss served the first match of his suspension as South Africa suffered a 20-17 defeat to Ireland.

Unable to attend the match, Erasmus instead hosted an online watchalong for supporters.

The South African, citing reporting from The Times, revealed that a formal challenge had still not been lodged.

The publication raised the possibility that SA Rugby had quietly accepted the punishment.

Further reporting from The42 indicated that SA Rugby had still not followed through on its public announcement with a formal request for a hearing.

Meanwhile, the Springboks boss could face another disciplinary headache after it emerged that Erasmus could face an even longer ban from World Rugby following comments made during his watchalong.

Ten days after the original suspension was announced, there is still no public confirmation of a hearing.

Erasmus is set to serve the second match of his ban against France on Sunday, leaving four internationals outstanding heading into 2027.

Despite SA Rugby's swift response to the original punishment, the Springboks boss looks increasingly likely to serve his suspension in full.

Neither governing body has officially confirmed that the matter is closed.

title: Familiar faces and surprise chances as Ireland face Wallabies
article_text:
Discussion about how Ireland head coach Andy Farrell would approach Friday's Nations Championship fifth-place play-off against Australia was ended emphatically by the team announcement on Wednesday.

While Farrell would have been excused for fielding a rotated side in the wake of last week's bruising victory over world champions South Africa, he instead opted for continuity and is challenging his first-choice line-up to produce another chest-thumping 80-minute display against the Wallabies.

Farrell has made two changes from the side that started Saturday's 20-17 success over the Springboks in Dublin, both of which are enforced.

Jacob Stockdale replaces the ill Mack Hansen on the left wing while in-form back row Nick Timoney is restored at number eight in place of the banned Dan Sheehan.

While Ireland cannot win the inaugural Nations Championship, Farrell has emphasised the importance of Friday in the context of the team's journey to next year's World Cup.

Victory over Australia - who they beat 33-31 in Sydney in July - would be four wins in as many weekends. Do that down under next year and Ireland will find themselves in another World Cup quarter-final.

The six-day turnaround between last week's win over South Africa and Friday's contest with Australia serves as useful preparation for next year's tournament, where Ireland will have six days between their pool games against Portugal and Scotland and potentially a quarter and semi-final, should they reach that stage.

With no six-day turnarounds in the 2027 Six Nations, Farrell is keen to test his side within those parameters before they return to their provinces for a busy festive schedule.

While the World Cup unavoidably edges into view, Ireland's immediate priority is to close out a largely positive 2026 on a winning note.

Sobering defeats by France and New Zealand cast doubts over the squad's trajectory, but last week's narrow win over South Africa served as a reminder that Farrell's side can still mix it with the world's best.

And while slaying the Springboks may have restored hope among fans, senior squad figures have carefully tempered expectations as they attempt to round out the year with a 10th win from 12 Tests.

"If you're winning games by the skin of your teeth and not performing well you don't really gain that belief, but when you're playing well and then start winning well the belief comes and that's something that we certainly gained before the 2023 World Cup," said Tadhg Beirne, who will captain Ireland against Australia in Sheehan's absence.

"But we're building that and we're often talking about that in terms of creating that belief, creating that identity that we want to see of ourselves, but again we're nowhere near where we need to be if we want to be competing to win a World Cup next year.

"I think there's so much more growth but we have to keep delivering in these big games for everyone to feel it and I know how it feels back in 2023 going into that World Cup.

"I think everyone in that squad felt it and I think we're certainly on the way there and if we can keep performing the way we've been performing but getting better we'll certainly be there by next year."

Friday night is a big opportunity for Stockdale, who was not involved in the wins over Argentina, Fiji and South Africa.

Nearly nine years removed from his star-making performances for Joe Schmidt's Ireland in the 2018 Grand Slam campaign, the 30-year-old Ulster wing is no longer a nailed-on starter.

But having been picked ahead of Tommy O'Brien - who scored two tries in the win over Fiji - Stockdale must seize an opportunity to impress on what will be his first run-out at Twickenham since a try-scoring cameo off the bench in a behind-closed-doors Autumn Nations Cup defeat by England in November 2020.

Stockdale needn't look far for inspiration. Seven of his Ulster team-mates are in the matchday 23. Two of them - Stuart McCloskey and Timoney - have featured in all 12 Tests this year (alongside Beirne), while jet-heeled right winger Robert Baloucoune is enjoying his best run as an international after a couple of tries against South Africa last week.

In January 2016, Stockdale made his Ulster debut under the province's then director of rugby Les Kiss, the man now leading the Wallabies.

The 61-year-old replaced Schmidt following the July leg of the Nations Championship, and while scrutiny on the Queenslander intensified following defeats by England and Scotland, last week's 29-26 victory over Wales has boosted the Wallaby morale as they attempt to snap a six-game losing streak against the Irish.

Kiss, who was Ireland's defence coach during the historic 2009 Grand Slam triumph, has turned heads with his own selection in the number 11 jersey, with former Northampton Saints winger James Ramm earning his Test debut at the age of 28.

Kurtley Beale - who started Australia's last victory over Ireland in June 2018 - is an eye-catching addition to the bench as the 37-year-old closes in on a first Test cap in five years.

With Kalani Thomas earning a first start at scrum-half and a new back-row combination in Tom Hooper, Carlo Tizzano and Rob Valetini, it is an intriguing Wallabies line-up.

But if Ireland can replicate the intensity and edge they showed against South Africa, they may pass Farrell's World Cup rehearsal and ensure they approach the tantalising possibilities of 2027 in buoyant form.

title: Three international rugby coaches banned in the space of just eight days
article_text:
Three international rugby coaches, including Springboks boss Rassie Erasmus, have been handed bans totalling 14 matches in the space of just eight days.

World Rugby has stepped up its crackdown on misconduct towards match officials, with coaches from South Africa, Hong Kong China and Romania all sanctioned this November.

The biggest name on the list is Erasmus, who could face an even longer ban following a fresh World Rugby investigation.

However, the Springboks boss is not alone, with a former All Blacks international also receiving a lengthy suspension.

RUCK takes a look at the three international coaches banned this month and the reasons behind their punishments.

The Springboks boss was handed a six-match suspension on 17 November following controversial comments about the officiating during South Africa's 21-19 defeat to France.

An independent panel concluded that his remarks questioned the integrity of match officials and met the threshold for serious misconduct.

The suspension prevents Erasmus from attending matches, carrying out match-day coaching duties or communicating with his players and coaching team on match days.

SA Rugby has indicated that Erasmus will challenge the decision through a full misconduct hearing.

Former All Blacks prop and Hong Kong China scrum coach Kane Hames received a six-match suspension on the same day as Erasmus.

Hames was performing water carrier duties during his side's Nations Cup clash against the United States on 8 November.

The live television broadcast picked up several instances of offensive language directed towards match officials.

His suspension prohibits him from taking part in any match-day activities, including attending the stadium.

Romania defence coach Benjamin Lapeyre became the latest casualty of the crackdown on 25 November.

The Frenchman repeatedly challenged officiating decisions while acting as a water carrier during Romania's 27-26 defeat to Canada.

An independent panel ruled that his conduct amounted to a failure to respect the authority of the officials.

He has subsequently been banned from all match-day activities for two games.

World Rugby introduced its Match Official Abuse Sanction Process in July 2026.

The system allows independent panels to issue warnings or automatic suspensions for unacceptable conduct towards officials.

World Rugby believes that irresponsible comments from influential figures within the sport can fuel online abuse of referees.

With three coaches sanctioned in just eight days, the governing body is demonstrating its willingness to enforce the new measures.

title: Flying Fijians make nine changes to starting XV for Italy rematch
article_text:
Fiji head coach Jake White has made nine changes to the team that beat Italy last week for this weekend’s rematch at Twickenham in the sixth versus sixth Nations Championship playoff.

Last week’s 21-16 win in Udine was Fiji’s first of the Nations Championship, but without a bonus point in the Test, they were unable to climb off the bottom of the Southern Hemisphere ladder. Italy were already locked into last place in the Northern Hemisphere.

For the rematch, white has brought in a new front row for the first time in November, promoting Vilikesa Nairau, Peniami Narisia and Inoke Ravuiwasa to the starting unit. Tevita Ikanivere drops to the bench, alongside usual running mates Peni Ravai and Luke Tagi, as Isoa Nasilasila assumes captaincy. Elia Canakaivata replaces Nathan Hughes in the starting loose forward trio and Etonia Waqa keeps his place on the bench.

In the backline, Terio Tamani swaps his bench role for Frank Lomani’s starting position, and Caleb Muntz is also moved into the starting team at 10. Vinaya Habosi and Iosefo Masi become the starting midfield duo, with Peniasi Dakuwaqa selected on the left wing.

“We were obviously very happy with the win,” White said.

“We also know we weren’t playing as well as we can. All I’m expecting is that the way we played and the opportunities we created, we do the same thing, but we need to be a little bit more accurate and a little bit more brave. I just don’t want the players to go into that game and not fire a shot.”

title: Rennie quizzed on All Blacks selections and rotation amid injuries and fatigue
article_text:
With back-to-back historic losses and plenty of talk about fatigue at the back-end of the All Blacks‘ season, head coach Dave Rennie has faced a string of direct questions as his team approach of their final Test of the year.

The All Blacks arrive at the Nations Championship bronze-medal match hoping to avoid equaling 1949’s record for most losses in a single season, while aiming to reverse their recent momentum and claim third place at the inaugural tournament.

More than a dozen All Blacks are unavailable for the Test through injury, and a viral quote from selector Graham Henry this week has pointed to heavy fatigue in the squad as a major factor in losses to Wales and England over the past fortnight.

Both points raise questions over Rennie’s selection and rotation throughout the season, but the coach wasn’t willing to validate the noise ahead of this weekend’s Test.

“Look, a lot of talk about fatigue, but we’ll worry about fatigue next week,” he said. “Everyone understands the expectation when you wear the jersey, and so the boys are keen as.”

Even with the latest injuries and talk of fatigue, Saula Ma’u, Chay Fihaki and Josh Jacomb are yet to feature on the tour, while injury replacements Sam Darry and Billy Proctor also remain in the background.

“Look, ideally you want everyone to play,” Rennie said of his young squad members. “It’s based on where we’re at. I often talk about earning the right to play, and they’re in some really competitive spots. We’ve tried to put out a team that we believe is strong enough to win, and we did that last week, and that’s what we’re doing again this week.”

With his first year as All Blacks head coach nearly complete, Rennie’s focus was on the learnings he and his men can take from the campaign.

“I mean, you learn, don’t you? And probably really good for us getting these learnings a long way out (from the World Cup). We’ve used an enormous amount of players, so we’ve got a really good understanding of a wide base of potential All Blacks for a World Cup next year, and it’s going to put us in a pretty strong place heading into Super Rugby in regard to players being really clear on the shifts they need to make or what they need to nail to be going to a World Cup.

“We’ve sat down with all the players, and we’ve gone through what we call PEPs, which are performance plans. We completed the last of those a couple of nights ago, and so we’re really clear on where the boys are at and what we think they need to do. They’re really clear on what’s important for us and their jobs to actually drive their development, and take that back to Super Rugby.

“And so, like as I’ve said, we’ve played about 60 players, and only 33 will go to a World Cup, so I think we’re in a good position because of that.”

When asked whether any players had played their way out of a World Cup selection, Rennie wouldn’t entertain the question: “I mean, I’m not going to answer that. We’re certainly not thinking that way”.

“When you’re put under a little bit of pressure, you reflect a lot. So we’ll have, post this game, a fair bit of time to reflect on what needs to be better, and then our connection with the Super Rugby teams and players over that period will be really important.”

title: 'Unbelievable achievement': Barrett legacy grows with latest All Blacks captaincy nod
article_text:
All Blacks head coach Dave Rennie says it was a “pretty simple” decision to name Jordie Barrett captain for this weekend’s Nations Championship bronze final after losing Codie Taylor to a calf injury.

Earlier this year, Barrett co-captained the Hurricanes to a Super Rugby Pacific title alongside Du’Plessis Kirifi, and has since played a growing role in the All Blacks’ leadership group.

Barrett has played 88 Tests for New Zealand and was recently named a finalist for World Rugby Player of the Year, but has never captained the All Blacks before. His maiden opportunity in the captain’s armband comes after injuries to Ardie Savea, Luke Jacobson and Will Jordan, all before Taylor went down in last weekend’s historic defeat to England.

“We’ve all lost a little bit of experience, but got a really excited group taking the field on Saturday,” Rennie said, reflecting on his injury list.

“It’s been interesting this week because I’d spoken to Codie when we decided Codie was going to be unavailable. I told him we’re going to make Jordie captain, and he said, ‘Oh, can I tell him?’ And so Codie was quite emotional when he passed that information on to Jordie.

“It was a pretty simple choice for us. I think anyone who would have worked with Jordie would know he’s very impressive; he has great game understanding, both sides of the ball, and is prepared to challenge. So he’s been great in our leadership group, and he’s taken over the captaincy role when Codie left the field last week and a couple of weeks ago. So that was a pretty straightforward decision for us.”

Jordie becomes the third Barrett sibling to captain the All Blacks, following older brother Scott, who led the team for the past two years under Scott Robertson, and Beauden, who assumed the role when Taylor was rested two weeks ago in Cardiff. All three brothers have been named in the matchday 23, with Beauden on the bench while Jordie and Scott start.

“Look, it’s an unbelievable achievement for the Barrett family, isn’t it? But we’re doing it because our opinion is that he (Jordie) is the right man for the job,” Rennie added.

“His challenge is going to be getting the best out of everyone around him, because he very much carries the team on his back; he’s the one who flies out and gives you line speed, and he chases things. So with the extra responsibility of captaincy, he’s going to have to be really good at getting the best of others, and I’m sure he can deliver on that challenge.”

title: Why Jonah Lomu’s son chose Six Nations side over the All Blacks
article_text:
Jonah Lomu’s two sons are doing their dad proud, with the youngsters continuing his incredible legacy more than a decade after the rugby icon’s tragic death.

Brayley and Dhyreille Lomu have grown up carrying one of the most famous surnames in world rugby.

However, despite their father's legendary status with the All Blacks, the brothers once revealed they would rather represent a Six Nations country.

The younger of the two even earned the nickname ‘Frenchie’ growing up in New Zealand.

The Lomu family has a deep affection for France, where Jonah spent part of his playing career with Marseille.

Dhyreille was born in the French city in September 2010, making the country particularly special to him.

In 2017, the brothers visited France's national rugby training base at Marcoussis as part of the country's successful bid to host the 2023 Rugby World Cup.

When asked whether they dreamed of becoming All Blacks, their response was simple.

Their mother, Nadene, also described France as the family's second home, explaining how much Jonah loved the country.

However, neither brother has formally committed to an international rugby nation.

Rather than feeling pressure to match their father's remarkable achievements, both brothers have pursued ambitions in professional tennis.

Their grandfather, Mervyn Quirk, helped coach them, while the youngsters switched to remote schooling to dedicate more time to their training.

Speaking to 1News in 2021, Dhyreille gave a touching explanation for wanting to follow a different sporting path.

“Dad will always be the best and I thought to maybe give something else a try cause I’ll never be better than him.”

The brothers are now helping to create something special away from competitive sport.

Alongside their mother, they have helped launch The Jonah Lomu Foundation, supporting young people who have experienced the loss of a parent.

Brayley previously explained why the project means so much to them.

“We know what it means to lose a parent and still hold on to big dreams.”

The family's next major milestone comes on December 12 and 13, when Auckland will host the inaugural Lomu Legacy International Under-18 Sevens Tournament.

The event will give young rugby players an international stage on which to showcase their talents while celebrating their father's legacy.

Jonah Lomu will always be remembered for his 37 tries in 63 Tests for the All Blacks and his unforgettable Rugby World Cup performances.

Through Brayley and Dhyreille, however, his legacy is becoming about much more than rugby.

The two boys are doing their dad proud in their own special way.
