Combine business intelligence and editorial excellence to reach engaged professionals across 36 leading media platforms.

However, home games of Belgian sides in the competitions are listed as protected events under Belgian legislation, meaning they must be covered FTA domestically.

This presented an opportunity for VTM (Dutch-language FTA) and RTL (French-language FTA), which have held the UEFA Champions League rights in the country throughout the 2024-27 cycle, to not only retain those rights going forward, but expand with the Europa League rights.

VTM, alongside the Belgian teams’ games, will also showcase the semi-finals and finals of the Champions League and Europa League through the deal.

The losers, in this case, are the current rights holders for the Europa League, namely VRT and RTBF (both FTA), as well as Telenet on an exclusive Dutch-language basis, and pay-TV's BeTV.

Perhaps conspicuously, the Conference League rights are not included in the deal, although Belgian teams still compete in the competition, indicating that Canal+ may seek a further sub-licensing agreement for that competition, perhaps with the aforementioned VRT, RTBF, and Telenet.

Further to the UEFA element, DPG Media and RTL will also showcase Canal+ entertainment programming across their platform, and conversely, will allow Canal+ to distribute its channels on its own platform, and the three will collaborate to invest in content.

Speaking on the announcement, Canal+ chief executive for Benelux (Belgium, Netherlands, and Luxembourg) and Central Europe Yassine Bouzoubaa said: “By joining forces, we are going far beyond a distribution agreement to strengthen our offering and make it more accessible to Belgian audiences. This partnership is a key step towards making Canal+ a leading player in Belgian media and entertainment.”

Canal+ group operates in Belgium through its subsidiaries Télésat (primarily French-speaking) and TV Vlaanderen (Flanders region).

Currently, five Belgian teams are competing in European competition: Club Brugge in the Champions League, Royal Union Saint-Gilloise and Anderlecht in the Europa League, and Sint-Truidense V.V. and Gent in the Conference League.

title: NZ SailGP team hires former All Blacks exec Guthrie as commercial chief
article_text:
The New Zealand SailGP team has appointed former New Zealand Rugby executive Yarnie Guthrie as its new chief commercial officer.

In the role, he will lead the team’s commercial strategy and partnerships in New Zealand and around the world.

Combine business intelligence and editorial excellence to reach engaged professionals across 36 leading media platforms.

He will work alongside new ownership group MSP Sports Capital and co-CEOs Peter Burling and Blair Tuke, the Olympic champions who founded the team.

The appointment comes five months after MSP acquired a majority stake in the team, also known as the Black Foils.

On Guthrie’s appointment, Burling said: “Yarnie’s spent years building partnerships for the All Blacks and Black Ferns, and that’s exactly the experience we want behind the Black Foils.

“To have someone of his calibre leading our commercial work says a lot about how far we’ve come as a team. I’m looking forward to working with him to bring new partners on board and do more with the ones who already back us.”

Guthrie joined New Zealand Rugby in 2016 to run the commercial programme for the 2017 British & Irish Lions tour. He went on to lead partnerships and global commercial sales, working with the All Blacks and Black Ferns, before becoming general manager of commercial in 2023.

He previously spent six years as commercial director of Welsh rugby side the Ospreys.

Guthrie joins the team in Abu Dhabi this week for the Abu Dhabi Sail Grand Prix on November 28 and 29, the final event of the 2026 SailGP season.

Jeff Moorad, CEO of MSP Sports Capital, added: “Yarnie brings an exceptional track record of building commercial partnerships and driving growth for one of the world’s most recognised sporting brands.

“We see tremendous opportunity to grow the Black Foils’ commercial platform, deepen our relationships with partners and connect with fans in New Zealand and around the world.”

title: Wales end Nations Championship with hearty Japan win
article_text:
Wales finished their Nations Championship campaign with another victory against Japan in a six-try display at the Allianz Stadium in Twickenham.

Wing Josh Adams and replacement flanker Jac Morgan claimed two tries apiece, with full-back Blair Murray and scrum-half Reuben Morgan-Williams also dotting down, while player of the match Sam Costelow kicked 10 points.

This set up the most comprehensive margin of victory of the Steve Tandy coaching era in a match that was affected by the miserable conditions.

Despite the scoreline, Wales again spent large periods of the game defending against a weakened Japan side who managed two late tries through replacements Shinya Komura and Halatoa Vailea.

Returning flanker James Botham made 38 tackles as he equalled Dafydd Jenkins' world record effort in the 35-28 win against New Zealand, a mark they now both share with Thierry Dusautoir of France.

It was a curious contest, low on quality, played in front of a half-empty Twickenham as part of a double-header before England faced New Zealand.

The victory means Wales secured ninth in the inaugural Nations Championship and finished the year ninth in World Rugby's rankings.

It was a second win in the space of three weeks against Japan, and a third victory in a November campaign that will forever be remembered for Wales beating New Zealand for the first time in 73 years.

Wales had unconvincingly defeated Japan 28-21 in the opening game of the November series, following up that with the famous win against the All Blacks before a narrow loss to Australia.

Both Wales and Japan had finished fifth in their respective hemisphere sections to set up a fifth contest between Wales and Japan inside 17 months.

Eddie Jones' side had suffered heavy 60-point defeats to England and Scotland and were down to the bare bones with flanker Tiennan Costley named on the wing.

Wales initially made five changes with Morgan-Williams making his first Test start and prop Rhys Carre, hooker Ryan Elias, lock Adam Beard and Botham also included.

With hooker Dewi Lake and Morgan dropping to the bench, lock Dafydd Jenkins captained the side for the first time in more than two years.

There was another late alteration when wing Louis Rees-Zammit was ruled out because of illness, with Scarlets back Ellis Mee promoted from the bench for his first action of this November campaign.

With tickets sold for both games there was a sparse crowd when the two sides came out and there was the unusual sound of being able to hear the players on the field when the match started.

After the Principality Stadium cauldrons of the past couple of weeks, Tandy told his side they had to create their own atmosphere and energy.

Number eight Aaron Wainwright followed that advice by producing a charging run from the kick-off, but Morgan-Williams kicked the ball straight into touch before another poor effort in a nervy start for the Ospreys man.

Japan were sharper in the early exchanges with co-captains Naoto Saito and Warner Dearns breaking the Wales defence and wing Koga Nezuka almost wriggling through.

Fly-half Riku Kitahara missed an attacking kick to touch and the momentum changed.

Wales' attacking kicking game proved fruitful in the first half and helped create the opening four tries.

Mee produced a towering high-ball take before fellow wing Adams dotted down for a try after collecting a Sam Costelow cross-kick.

Wales caught Japan on the counter-attack with a kick from centre James expertly picked up and finished by Murray.

James provided another unlikely kick assist with Adams this time the beneficiary for his second score.

Wales' defence continued to be tested and it required a thundering double tackle from Jenkins and James to deny Japan, with Botham then turning over the ball.

Botham has had an eventful couple of weeks. After being named player of the match against New Zealand, he was left out against Australia, a decision that his father took to social media to criticise.

Botham was present at the birth of his child earlier this week before coming back in for the Japan game.

His Cardiff back-row colleague Alex Mann gave away a silly offside penalty but Japan were again denied.

In tricky conditions, a period of distinct mediocrity followed from both sides before Morgan-Williams started and finished the move that led to Wales' fourth try and his first international score.

That looked like becoming his second soon after as Morgan-Williams cantered over following good work from Mann, but the move was called back for a knock-on from prop Archie Griffin.

Wales' defensive defiance continued when Mee's foot somehow denied Japan's Charlie Lawrence from grounding the ball.

Beard was shown a yellow card for Wales' persistent offending in their own 22 and flanker Ben Gunter appeared to have broken the Welsh resistance, but his score was ruled out by the television match official (TMO).

Wales led 26-0 at half-time but the statistics heavily favoured Japan.

Tandy's side only had 32% possession and 25% territory and made 160 tackles to 45 compared to Japan, who made 121 carries compared to Wales' 55.

The lack of quality and Wales' defending again dominated the early second-half exchanges.

Wales made four changes, including the introduction of Lake and Morgan, who scored within a few seconds of coming on from a driving maul.

Morgan doubled that when he powered over from a tap-penalty move.

Tom Rogers' wait for his first Test chance since scoring a hat-trick against New Zealand 12 months ago ended when he came on for Murray.

title: Farrell says low Twickenham crowd in Ireland win 'a shame'
article_text:
Ireland head coach Andy Farrell said it was a "shame" his side's Nations Championship victory over Australia was played in front of a low crowd at Twickenham's Allianz Stadium.

Friday night's fifth-place play-off attracted an attendance of just 32,000 with the uppermost tier of the 82,000-capacity stadium entirely closed.

Ireland beat the Wallabies 38-14 after Italy overcame Fiji on the first day of the inaugural competition's finals day weekend at the home of England rugby.

Ticket sales for Saturday and Sunday's action, which are headlined by England v New Zealand and the final between South Africa and France, have been stronger, but Farrell questioned the Friday night double-bill.

"I'd love to spend some time to have a think about it, I've been preparing a team and you're busy doing that," he said.

"But off the top of my head, I don't know whether the Friday night thing works or being at the same venue. If we'd have played at the Aviva (Stadium in Dublin), it would have been full.

"They look like little things, but they're not, they mean a lot to the fans, like when you don't know where your team's playing and then you're trying to get a flight and all of a sudden they're £1,700. It doesn't fit."

Farrell said he enjoyed parts of the spectacle, which included a pre-game performance from British popstar Myles Smith.

"I love what they're trying to do. I love the razzmatazz and coming into the ground it felt different. It felt like it was trying to be like an event, like a concert," he added.

"It was just a shame that we couldn't get the people through the door. The pre-match hype looked fantastic on the TV – from what I saw in the dressing room anyway.

"The 16:40 game – I felt for those boys really. And Sam Prendergast didn't get anything for man of the match, so playing for fifth place obviously didn't mean much."

Ireland won five of their six pool games to finish third in the northern hemisphere table behind France and England, while Australia finished third in the southern hemisphere standings behind South Africa and New Zealand after losing four matches.

"It's strange, it doesn't make sense," Farrell said.

"But it's not our jobs to make sense of it. It's our job to just keep playing what's in front of our faces."

While Farrell was left unconvinced by parts of the finals weekend, Rugby Football Union (RFU) chief executive Bill Sweeney said organisers are pleased with the first edition of the competition while admitting "tweaks" are needed in the future.

"We knew Friday was going to be a tough sell," Sweeney told ITV.

"I think we had just over 30 (thousand) here last night but when you consider we've sold over 160,000 tickets over three days for an inaugural tournament where a lot of us bought blind when frankly people didn't know what the match-ups were going to be, we're really pleased with that.

"When you look at the TV viewership, we should get over 100 million people watching this, so that's 170% up on where we were with the autumns, so we're really happy."

title: Five-try Ireland beat Australia in autumn finale
article_text:
Ireland secured a fifth-place finish in the inaugural Nations Championship thanks to a 38-14 victory over Australia in London.

While last week's 20-17 win over South Africa was the undoubted highlight of their campaign, victory on Friday night ensured Ireland won all four games they played in November.

After Italy narrowly beat Fiji in the first game of the day, Ireland started slowly in a sparsely populated Allianz Stadium with the Wallabies taking a deserved lead through Jeremy Williams' try.

Andy Farrell's side took control of the contest through 24 unanswered points either side of half-time with Robbie Henshaw, Nick Timoney and Robert Baloucoune crossing for scores, while Sam Prendergast converted all three and added a penalty.

Kalani Thomas briefly stalled Ireland's momentum, but replacement back row James McNabney marked his second cap with a pair of tries in the final seven minutes to give the number two side in the world a comfortable, if not always convincing, victory.

After what was their final Test match of 2026, Ireland finish the year with a record of 10 wins and two losses from 12 internationals.

After making only two forced changes from the side who beat the Springboks six days ago - the banned Dan Sheehan and ill Mack Hansen the ones to miss out - head coach Farrell had called on his squad to back up their performance against the reigning world champions.

The early stages, however, had none of the tempo or accuracy from last week in the Aviva Stadium. Sloppy knock-ons, coupled with a pair of scrum penalties, saw Ireland struggle to gain a foothold in the contest.

For all Australia's territory and possession, the Wallabies took until the 23rd minute to press home their advantage on the scoreboard.

Previously undone by a couple of kicking errors, Les Kiss' side looked most dangerous when keeping the ball tight and it was lock Williams who burrowed over for the game's opening score.

Australia's deserved lead, however, lasted just three minutes. A midfield penalty allowed Prendergast to kick for the corner and give Ireland their first visit to the opposition 22.

After a sharp attack down the short side was thwarted before the line, Ireland came back inside and Stuart McCloskey spun out of a tackle well to put his centre partner Henshaw over for the try.

Three minutes before the break, again aided by an Australia penalty, Ireland doubled their lead.

Tadhg Beirne did well to gather a line-out with one hand and, with Ireland's centres joining the maul, number eight Timoney broke off the base for the simple score.

Prendergast converted both scores and added a penalty with the last kick of the half to put Ireland in a commanding 10-point lead at the break despite their shaky start.

If Ireland started slowly in the first half, they flew from the traps after the restart.

Jacob Stockdale had already almost executed a fine chip-and-chase reminiscent of his best days in the green jersey before his Ulster team-mate Baloucoune scored Ireland's third in the 43rd minute.

Baloucoune, 29, gathered Prendergast's measured cross-field kick over the head of James Ramm to score his fifth try of the autumn.

Australia threw everything at getting back into the game but a penalty for coming in at the side, which halted a 19-phase attack under the posts, summed up a frustrating evening with ball in hand for next year's World Cup hosts.

Scrum-half Thomas did score his first international try to reduce Ireland's lead to 24-14 with 25 minutes to go, but a comeback never felt likely from an Australia side who used Kurtley Beale from the bench for the utility back's first cap in five years.

While the game lost further shape in the final quarter with the arrival of a glut of replacements, Ulster's McNabney caught the eye in a short cameo.

Having had his debut against Fiji cut short by a head injury two weeks ago, the back row was the beneficiary of a fearsome Irish scrum shortly before his first try and then finished things off with another close-range score in the final minute.

Ireland: Keenan; Baloucoune, Henshaw, McCloskey, Stockdale; Prendergast, Gibson-Park; Porter, Kelleher, Furlong, McCarthy, Beirne (capt), Baird, Van der Flier, Timoney.

Replacements: Stewart, O'Toole, Clarkson, Ryan, McNabney, Doak, Frawley, Aki.

Australia: Wright; Jorgensen, Suaalii, Ikitau, Ramm; Gordon, Thomas; Kailea, Paenga-Amosa, Alaalatoa (co-capt), Canham, Williams, Hooper, Tizzano, Valetini.

Replacements: Nasser, Bell, Tupou, Shaw, Wilson (co-capt), McReight, Wilson, Beale.

title: Andy Farrell questions Nations Championship finals weekend format: ‘It doesn’t make sense’
article_text:
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

The Ireland head coach Andy Farrell has questioned the format and scheduling of the Nations Championship finals weekend after the opening night of the inaugural edition fell flat.

Farrell’s side were impressive in holding Australia at bay before surging away to a 38-14 win, but there was a limited crowd in attendance at Twickenham’s Allianz Stadium for Friday’s double header.

Italy had earlier beaten Fiji in the first of six games in one weekend at the ground, with two more days of back-to-back games to follow on Saturday and Sunday.

There was confusion, too, over what the sides were actually playing for, with both Farrell and Wallabies counterpart Les Kiss making reference to battling for fifth place – even though competition organisers were insistent that was not the case.

Ireland are ranked second in the world and lost just once in the competition, finishing with more points than South Africa – who will contest the grand final on Sunday having topped the southern hemisphere pool.

Farrell believes the format needs looking at before the next edition in 2028.

“I’d love to spend some time to have some time to think about it, but off the top of my head, I don’t know whether the Friday night thing works, or the same venue or whatever,” he explained. “If we would have played at the Aviva [Stadium], it would have been full tonight.

“Obviously, these look like little things but they mean a lot to the fans as far as you don’t know when a team is playing, and you are trying to find a flight and all of a sudden they are £1700. It doesn’t fit. I love what they are trying to do. I love the razzmatazz. Coming into the ground definitely felt different. It felt like it was trying to be like an event, like a concert or whatever. It was just a shame we couldn’t get the people through the door. It’ll be interesting, now – the 20 to 5 game [Italy vs Fiji], I felt for those boys, really.”

When pressed on whether he felt fans would be confused by Ireland enjoying a successful campaign but having little to show for it, Farrell added: “It’s strange, isn’t it? It doesn’t make sense. But it’s not our job to make sense of it. It’s our job to just keep playing what is in front of us.”

Overall, the Ireland boss is a fan of the revamp of the July and November international windows – though thinks it will take time to bed in.

“I think everyone has been interested in it. Certainly in the autumn when everyone knows a little bit more how the land lies and the points needed to progress to the finals weekend, it certainly hypes that up. I think you have seen the results of that. I think we’ll get a better sense of it when it is not a World Cup year.

“When a competition starts in July, you are always going to get teams at different stages of growth in their squad. It will be interesting to see what it will be like after the World Cup year to see the difference as far as that is concerned.”

Paris is thought to be a strong contender to host the 2028 finals, while Spain are also known to be keen to be considered as a destination in the future having bid for the 2035 Rugby World Cup.

Organisers are expected to take an in-depth look at the finals weekend for future editions.

title: GB miss out on Davis Cup final as Alcaraz stars for Spain
article_text:
Great Britain were unable to give Leon Smith the perfect send-off as Davis Cup captain as Carlos Alcaraz inspired Spain to a 2-0 victory in the semi-finals.

Competing in their first Davis Cup semi-final since 2019, Britain fell short as Arthur Fery was unable to match the dazzling brilliance of Alcaraz, with the seven-time major winner surging to an emphatic 6-2 6-1 win.

That was after rising star Rafael Jodar defeated Cameron Norrie 6-2 7-5 in the opening singles match to put Spain in the driving seat in Bologna.

The defeat brings the curtain down on Smith's near 17-year tenure as captain, during which he led Britain to Davis Cup success in 2015.

Spain captain David Ferrer, who is also stepping down after this year's tournament, will have the chance to guide his nation to their first Davis Cup title since 2019 when they face Italy in Sunday's final.

Three-time defending champions Italy beat Spain in last year's final, although they are without talisman and world number two Jannik Sinner because of a knee injury that will keep him out of the Australian Open.

"It is a second straight final, it is going to be my first Davis Cup final, I'll do whatever it takes to win," said Alcaraz.

"It's something I have been chasing for a really long time, to be in a Davis Cup final."

After Norrie's defeat by Jodar, Fery was faced with the mammoth task of beating world number three Alcaraz - a player he had never faced before.

Alcaraz lifted his first ATP Finals title six days earlier, a triumph that completed his astonishing return to the sport following four months out with a wrist injury.

And his return to top form was on full display as he dismantled Fery, ranked 32nd, in a dominant first set in which he dropped just two points behind his first serve.

Alcaraz's movement and shot-making continued to dazzle the crowd in Italy and Fery could do little to stop the Spaniard's sprint to the finish line.

Alcaraz started the season by becoming the youngest man to complete the career Grand Slam with his Australian Open triumph, and now has the chance to end the year with his first Davis Cup title, one of the few trophies he has yet to win.

For Fery, who enjoyed his career-best season and a fairytale run to the Wimbledon semi-finals, it was another harsh reminder of the gulf in class between himself and the game's top players after he fell in straight sets to world number one Alexander Zverev in Thursday's quarter-final.

World number 10 Jodar has established himself as one of the brightest talents in men's tennis in 2026, having started the year outside the top 150.

In the past 12 months he has made his Grand Slam debut, won a first ATP title and experienced a meteoric rise up the rankings, which saw him qualify for the end-of-season ATP Finals, reserved for the year's top eight performing men.

He and Norrie sped through the opening games, holding serve until Jodar struck the first blow with a phenomenal cross-court return on the Briton's serve to take a 3-2 lead.

The young Spaniard doubled his advantage two games later when Norrie ended a 29-shot rally with a plant into the net and Jodar calmly served out the opening set after 32 minutes.

A double fault landed Norrie in bother early on, but he recovered well and broke back for 4-4 before Jodar regained control to restore his lead, wrap up the victory and maintain his 100% record in three meetings against the Briton.

Italy sealed their place in the final with a 2-1 victory over the Czech Republic on Friday as Lorenzo Musetti starred in both his singles and doubles match to keep their title defence alive.

title: Elena Rybakina schedule: Where will world No 1 play during 2027 WTA Tour season?
article_text:
Elena Rybakina enjoyed a fantastic 2026 campaign as she finished as the year-end No 1 and she will defend four trophies during the new campaign.

The Kazakh star kicked off the 2026 season at No 5 in the WTA Rankings, but was crowned year-end No 1 in November with her rise coming on the back of winning two Grand Slam titles and two WTA 500 events.

Rybakina started her year with the Australian Open title, beating Aryna Sabalenka in the final, and in September she became a three-time major winner after lifting the US Open trophy with another win over Sabalenka.

She also won the Stuttgart Open and Ningbo Open.

So let’s take a look at the events that the three-time Grand Slam winner could play during the 2027 season.

Rybakina will once again kick off her season at the WTA 500 event in Australia with organisers confirming she will feature for a third time.

She won the title on debut in 2024, but didn’t return to defend her title. She was back in 2026 and lost in the quarter-final.

The Kazakh star will be seeded No 1 at a Grand Slam for the first time in her career when she defends her Australian Open crown.

Rybakina beat second seed Iga Swiatek, fifth seed Jessica Pegula and top seed Sabalenka en route to the title in 2026.

The big-name players usually take a few weeks off after the Australian Open before heading to the Middle East.

Rybakina will look to win the WTA 1000 title for the first time in her career with her best performance coming in 2024 when she finished runner-up to Swiatek while she lost in the quarter-final in 2026.

The Qatar event is immediately followed by the second WTA 1000 in the United Arab Emirates with Rybakina’s best run being a semi-final appearance in 2025.

Players who enjoy deep runs at the Australian Open and Qatar often skip the second leg of the Middle Eastern WTA 1000 double.

The Sunshine Double kicks off in Indian Wells and Rybakina won the title in 2023 while she was a runner-up in 2026, losing against Sabalenka in the final.

The Kazakh star lost two consecutive finals in 2024 and 2025, but made an early exit in 2026 as she lost in the second round.

Rybakina usually kicks off her clay-court season at the prestigious Stuttgart event where the winner drives away with a brand new Porsche.

The 27-year-old is already the owner of two Porsche sports cars as she won the tournament in 2026 and 2024.

The clay season triple header kicks off with the Madrid Open and Rybakina is yet to crack the code in the Spanish capital as she hasn’t reached a final yet. In 2026, she lost in the semi-final.

The final event before the French Open, Rybakina won the WTA 1000 event in 2023 but then missed her title defence the following year. She was beaten by eventual champion Elina Svitolina in the quarter-final in 2026.

The Roland Garros trophy is the only thing standing between Rybakina and a Career Grand Slam and a Surface Slam as she has majors at the Australian Open, Wimbledon and the US Open.

But she doesn’t have the best of records in Paris, losing in the second round in 2026 while she is yet to make it past the quarter-final.

The three-time Grand Slam winner has kicked off her grass-court season in London the past two years.

She reached the quarter-final both in 2025 and 2026.

Some players prefer to play only one warm-up event between Roland Garros and Wimbledon, but Rybakina has also played in Berlin the last two years, losing in the last eight two years ago and in the second round a year later.

The 2022 champion is always a favourite heading to the grass-court Grand Slam and this year will be no different, although she has struggled there in recent years.

After reaching the quarter-final in 2023 and semi-final the following year, Rybakina has failed to reach the second in the two most recent editions.

Rybakina has in the past started her North American hard-court swing at the Washington DC Open, but most players head straight to Canada these days.

She finished runner-up to Swiatek in the 2026 final and was a semi-finalist in 2025 and 2023.

The WTA 1000 double-header ends in Ohio and Rybakina was a quarter-finalist in 2026 and a semi-finalist in 2024.

Rybakina will finish her 2027 Grand Slam season as the defending champion at Flushing Meadows.

Outside of her title in 2026, the Kazakh star had failed to make it past the fourth round in New York.

The world No 1 reached the semi-final of the WTA 1000 event on her debut in 2023, but then missed the 2024 edition before losing in the third round the next year and the second round in 2026.

The final WTA 1000 event of the year and Rybakina is expected to be return in 2027 after missing the 2026 edition due to injury. She has played only twice in Wuhan in 2019 and 2024, reaching the quarter-finals on both occasions.

Rybakina will look to make it a hat-trick of titles at the WTA 500 event after winning the event in 2025 and 2026.

The Kazakh player was a quarter-finalist in 2026 and a semi-finalist in 2026, but she didn’t finish the tournament on both occasions as she withdrew due to injury.

title: Syed Modi India International 2026 badminton: Tanvi Sharma makes second BWF World Tour final of the year
Many seeded players fall as quarterfinals are set in Cardiff
article_text:
The first day of main draw action at the YONEX Welsh International Open 2026 delivered several surprises, with some of the highest-seeded players and pairs already out of the tournament ahead of Saturday’s quarterfinals.

In men’s singles, Scotland’s Matthew Waring caused an upset by defeating Switzerland’s fourth seed Tobias Kuenzi 17-21, 21-16, 21-10. Kuenzi had been moved to the top of the draw following the withdrawal of the original top two seeds.

Chinese Taipei’s third seed Ting Yen-Chen also suffered an early exit, losing to England’s Ethan Rose 23-21, 14-21, 21-13. Rose went on to secure his place in the quarterfinals with a straight-games victory over Denmark’s Mikkel Langemark.

In men’s doubles, Norway’s Torjus Flaatten/Jonas Østhassel knocked out top seeds Yann Orteu/Minh Quang Pham from Switzerland, winning 21-18, 21-12.

The second, third and fourth seeds in men’s doubles also exited the tournament. Czechia’s Vojtěch Havlíček/Tomáš Švejda lost to England’s Oliver Baczala/Jonty Russ, while Sweden’s Mio Molin/Max Svensson were defeated by Chua Yue Chern/Alvaro Vazquez. Scotland’s Evan Kenny/Josh Taylor completed a difficult day for the seeded pairs by defeating Hungary’s Csanad Horvath/Miklos Kis-Kasza.

In mixed doubles, Ireland’s Scott Guildea/Rachael Darragh defeated the top-seeded German pair Patrick Volkmann/Franziska Volkmann 14-21, 21-17, 21-17.

There was another Austrian success in women’s doubles, where Serena Au Yeong/Aline Müller defeated Ireland’s second seeds Orla Flynn/Siofra Flynn in three games.

In women’s singles, the two highest seeds, Liao Jui-Chi and Milena Schnider, both advanced to the quarterfinals. However, fourth seed Sophia Noble suffered a defeat against Japan’s Yuzuno Watanabe, while Denmark’s Ann-Sofie Husher Ruus knocked out fifth seed Xu Wei from Austria.

The tournament continues tomorrow with the quarterfinals starting at 10am local time, followed by the semifinals at approximately 3pm.

You can follow all the action live and free on BadmintonEurope.tv.

title: Arnaud Merkle reaches Super 300 final in India
article_text:
France's Arnaud Merkle booked his place in tomorrow's final at the Syed Modi India International 2026 earlier today, reaching his first Super 300 final in four years.

Entering the tournament as the sixth seed, Merkle has produced several impressive performances throughout the week, securing his place in the final with a convincing 21-13, 21-16 semifinal victory.

Four years after reaching his last Super 300 final at this very same tournament in India, Merkle now has another opportunity to claim the title.

The Frenchman was understandably delighted following his semifinal victory, but his focus is already on tomorrow's final.

“I will try not to think too much, because I want to win the tournament and not just be in the final. I'm very happy to have another chance to play in a final. It is the last match, so it will be all in for sure. I will do everything I can to be on the winning side,” Merkle said.

In tomorrow's final, Merkle will face Indonesia's Richie Duta Richardo.

In women's doubles, both European pairs saw their campaigns come to an end at the semifinal stage. England's Abbygael Harris/Estelle van Leeuwen lost 13-21, 18-21 to Indonesia's Isyana Syahira Meida/Rinjani Kwinnara Nastine, while Ukraine's Polina Buhrova/Yevheniia Kantemyr fell to defending champions Treesa Jolly/Gayatri Gopichand of India, 21-13, 10-21, 12-21.

title: Buhrova/Kantemyr set up semifinal clash with India's top seeds
article_text:
Ukraine and England both have pairs in the women's doubles semifinals at the Syed Modi India International 2026.

Third seeds Polina Buhrova/Yevheniia Kantemyr came from a game down to win against India's eighth seeds Ashwini Bhat K./Shikha Gautam 13-21, 21-12, 22-20. Tomorrow they face the top seeds and home favourites, Treesa Jolly/Gayatri Gopichand Pullela.

England's Abbygael Harris/Estelle van Leeuwen beat sixth seeds Zi Yu Low/Noraqilah Maisarah 21-18, 10-21, 21-18. They play Indonesia's fourth seeds, Isyana Syahira Meida/Rinjani Kwinnara Nastine, for a place in the final.

In men's singles, Arnaud Merkle has reached the semifinals after second seed Lee Zii Jia retired with the Frenchman leading 21-16, 11-6. Lee had said this would be his last tournament of the year. Merkle plays Chinese Taipei's Zhe Ying Wu next.

Three other European pairs went out in the quarterfinals: England's Callum Hemming/Estelle van Leeuwen and Scotland's Alexander Dunn/Julie MacPherson in mixed doubles, and France's Margot Lambert/Camille Pognante in women's doubles.

title: Money owed and future plans: LIV Golf is dead but still present as DPWT season begins
article_text:
Before the ink was dry on LIV Golf’s obituary, Jon Rahm and Tyrrell Hatton, two of the rebel league’s biggest fish, had already hoisted trophies on the DP World Tour. The once-Saudi-backed league was sinking to the bottom of the sea and those who had once called LIV home were already looking toward the future.

That future will be on the DP World Tour to start. The PGA Tour has yet to decide on a path back for defectors, while the tour that LIV wanted to destroy will see Rahm, Hatton, Bryson DeChambeau and others tee it up in 2027, giving it a huge boost of talent and attention. But as the golf world moves toward unification in a post-LIV landscape, the remnants of the league’s tentacles still linger as players grapple with what was and what will be.

That has been on display this week in Australia, where the DP World Tour’s season is getting underway at the Australian PGA.

For all of LIV Golf’s failures, one of its biggest wins was the success it found in going to golf-starved markets like Australia, where local fans flocked to LIV Adelaide to watch some of the world’s best tee it up. LIV Adelaide is no longer, but at this week’s Australian PGA Championship, the former stars of that event — the members of LIV’s Australian team Ripper GC — turned the page after four years of plying their trade on a league that no longer exists.

Cam Smith left for LIV Golf shortly after winning the 2022 Open Championship. He was the No. 2-ranked player in the world at the time, and his defection was a big coup for LIV as the PGA Tour teetered. But Smith’s game has faltered since leaving for LIV. From Sept. 2022 to August 2023, Smith won three times on LIV and posted two top-10 finishes. He added another top-10 at the 2024 Masters, but he has made just three of 11 cuts in majors since and has just one top-10 while failing to win on LIV.

With LIV now withering away in bankruptcy court, Smith and eight others have agreed to a deal with the DP World Tour for invites into select tournaments in 2027 as he looks to claw his way back to the PGA Tour.

“I guess that’s the path. That’s where I want to be now for sure,” Smith told the Australian Associated Press this week about getting back to the PGA Tour. “DP’s given us a chance to kind of fulfill that. We’ll see how that goes. There’s plenty of good players out there and plenty of other guys that want to do the same thing, so it’s going to be difficult. But for sure that’s where I want to play.”

Right now, the top 10 players in the final DP World Tour standings who are not otherwise exempt earn PGA Tour cards. But as the PGA Tour prepares to shift to a two-tier model in 2028, the number of cards given to DP World Tour finishers could shrink. Rory McIlroy has said that only a “handful” of cards and spots in the Championship Series will be awarded each year, making the DP World Tour highly entertaining as top players who went to LIV fight for only a few coveted spots.

For Smith, who is not a full-time DP World Tour member at the moment, it’s a feat he knows will be difficult to do initially unless he rips off a win on the European circuit in one of his handful of starts.

“I think given what they’ve told me, I pretty much need to win this year to get membership,” Smith said. “It’s all still very blurry to me at the moment. There’s a lot of rules, but we’ll have a few opportunities and like I said, I’ve always managed to play pretty good down here, so why not start it off with a good one?”

Lucas Herbert, like Smith, agreed to a deal with the DP World Tour for select starts in 2027. The World No. 55 said he rejected the idea of joining LIV 2.0 because it didn’t give him access to major championships, and that’s his focus now. Like many former members of LIV Golf, Herbert still has money owed to him. But he isn’t counting on that landing in his account. He’ll have to deal with that in the background as he tries to put the entire saga behind him.

“Anything from this point is going to be a bonus,” Herbert told FOX Sports Australia. “It’s a long, drawn-out process with mostly lawyers winning out of the whole battle. I’ve accepted that and moved on. The reality is I made a lot of money at the same time as I’m owed a lot.

“As great as a time I had on the LIV tour, I had many legal issues along the way, which drew a lot of energy out of me. I’ve played this game a few times now and I’m going to expect not very much and hopefully be pleasantly surprised, rather than the other way around.”

While Smith and Herbert ready themselves for the grind of climbing back to the PGA Tour, former World No. 12 Marc Leishman is taking a different approach. The 43-year-old has often said he loved playing on LIV and that it let him spend more time with his family. He has fallen outside the top 300 in the world but thinks his time on LIV was worth it. He always knew that professional golf had an expiration date. He hopes he still has more left in the tank but he’s not sure what that looks like.

title: Bryson DeChambeau's agency lands major deal with group that tried to save LIV Golf
article_text:
BC Partners Credit, the same investment group that recently explored a $300 million rescue deal for LIV Golf, have made another significant move in professional golf after agreeing to acquire a majority stake in GSE Worldwide.

The transaction, structured as a growth equity investment, will see BC Partners take a controlling interest in the sports and entertainment agency from existing investor Gatemore Capital Management.

It represents an interesting development given BC Partners' recent involvement in LIV Golf, having ultimately walked away from a proposed $300 million financing and restructuring package that was intended to relaunch the breakaway league for the 2027 season.

That rescue plan collapsed after BC Partners failed to secure commitments from a critical mass of players willing to return for the proposed new-look circuit.

With its Saudi funding withdrawn and the restructuring deal falling apart, LIV Golf has now collapsed and entered a winding-down process, bringing an extraordinary chapter in professional golf to an end.

Now, rather than financing a potential LIV Golf revival, BC Partners have turned their attention towards another significant opportunity in the sport, acquiring a controlling interest in an agency with connections to some of professional golf's biggest names.

GSE Worldwide boasts an impressive roster of sporting talent, with its golf division representing former LIV Golf players Bryson DeChambeau and Joaquin Niemann, alongside PGA Tour pro Sam Burns.

The agency has developed into one of the world's leading sports and lifestyle representation businesses since Gatemore first invested in the company in 2018.

Through sustained organic growth and a series of strategic acquisitions, GSE has established an industry-leading golf and tennis talent representation business, while also expanding into the NFL, NBA and name, image and likeness (NIL) markets.

Its wider client portfolio includes sporting legends, broadcasters and personalities from the culinary world.

However, GSE's operations extend well beyond traditional athlete management.

The company has also developed a rapidly expanding events and experiential business, covering owned and operated properties, live event production, premium hospitality and brand activations.

These additional services have created further commercial opportunities for its athletes, brands and business partners, with GSE increasingly positioning itself as a major player across the wider sports and entertainment industry.

For professional golfers, that represents an increasingly important part of the modern sporting landscape, where commercial partnerships, personal branding, media opportunities and corporate relationships can be just as significant as on-course performances.

The acquisition also builds on an existing relationship between BC Partners Credit and GSE Worldwide.

Since 2024, BC Partners Credit has acted as the agency's senior lender and preferred equity investor, while also holding representation on its board.

The increased investment is a clear indication of the firm's confidence in GSE's future growth potential, with additional capital expected to support further acquisitions, organic expansion and investment across its various businesses.

Michael Principe, CEO of GSE Worldwide, said the expanded partnership would provide the company with greater resources to accelerate its ambitions.

"We've built GSE into one of the world's leading sports and entertainment agencies, and our ambitions for the future are even greater," Principe said.

He added that BC Partners had been a trusted partner over the past two years, with a strong understanding of the company's strategy and future opportunities.

The deal will allow GSE to pursue strategic acquisitions while continuing to invest in the people and businesses responsible for its growth.

Ted Goldthorpe, Head of BC Partners Credit and a member of the GSE Worldwide board, described the agency as an exceptional platform, highlighting its combination of talent representation, brand marketing, hospitality and live events.

He said BC Partners was excited to work alongside Principe and the wider management team to build on the foundations established over the past eight years.

For Gatemore Capital Management, the transaction marks the end of an eight-year investment in the business.

Managing Partner Liad Meidar described GSE's transformation into a top-ten global sports agency as a rewarding experience, adding that BC Partners was ideally positioned to support its next stage of growth.

While BC Partners' proposed LIV Golf rescue ultimately failed to materialise, its latest investment demonstrates that the firm remains committed to expanding its presence across the wider sports industry.

Having been unable to find a way to save the breakaway league, BC Partners have now secured a significant position in the business of professional golf through GSE Worldwide, an agency representing several of the sport's most recognisable players.

With DeChambeau, Niemann and Burns among its clients, the acquisition gives BC Partners an influential foothold in golf's commercial landscape at a time of significant change for the sport.

LIV Golf may have ended, but BC Partners are not walking away from the sport.

title: Lucas Herbert rips LIV Golf communication, says collapsed league owes him ‘a lot’
article_text:
Lucas Herbert is still playing golf — this week at the BMW Australia PGA Championship — so he isn't worried about what's happening with LIV Golf's legal proceedings, but he also isn’t counting on seeing all the money the league still owes him.

“You’re probably foolish to think you’re going to get much of it,” he told Fox Sports Australia on Friday.

“Anything from this point is going to be a bonus,” Herbert continued. “It’s a long drawn out process with mostly lawyers winning out of the whole battle. I’ve accepted that and moved on. The reality is I made a lot of money at the same time as I’m owed a lot.”

Herbert didn’t say exactly how much he is owed, but his comments provide another glimpse at the fallout from LIV’s demise after a turbulent final year that included the loss of its Saudi backing, a bankruptcy filing and, ultimately, liquidation.

“As great as a time I had on the LIV tour, I had many legal issues along the way, which drew a lot of energy out of me,” Herbert said. “I’ve played this game a few times now and I’m going to expect not very much and hopefully be pleasantly surprised, rather than the other way around.”

LIV’s problems became impossible to ignore when CEO Scott O’Neil acknowledged that funding from Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund was guaranteed only through the 2026 season. PIF later declined to continue funding a league that had spent nearly $6 billion in less than five years without developing enough television, sponsorship and commercial revenue to support itself.

The problems weren’t just financial, according to Herbert.

“I’ve got no problem saying we were poorly communicated with as players throughout the season,” he said.

“A lot of times mainstream media, or media outlets outside of LIV, knew more about what was going on than we did, which was pretty tough to deal with. It was a bit of a contributing factor as to why very few guys were interested in going around again in 2.0.”

By then, LIV was already losing some of the players who had helped give the league credibility. Brooks Koepka and Patrick Reed left before the season, and LIV failed to counter those departures with another wave of major signings.

Meanwhile, the financial pressure continued. LIV hired an investment bank as O’Neil worked to find outside financing. A technology company later sued LIV over more than $1 million in unpaid invoices and lost revenue.

The league eventually found a potential partner in BC Partners, which offered $300 million in funding for a scaled-down LIV 2.0 if the league could secure enough commitments from players.

After the season, LIV laid off much of its workforce and scaled back operations before filing for bankruptcy in early September. The proposed second act was supposed to feature smaller purses, smaller fields and a 10-event schedule, but players remained reluctant to commit.

Herbert said the uncertainty took its toll.

“It was a tough off-season to have everyone having an opinion on what your livelihood and career and future looks like when you don’t have control over (it) yourself,” Herbert said. “It’s one thing for people to have their opinions on your poor play, but it felt people at times took pride in seeing everything we tried to build at LIV fail.”

Once Jon Rahm decided to leave, more departures followed and confidence in LIV 2.0 evaporated. The league eventually shut down and moved to liquidate its remaining assets.

For Herbert, that leaves an uncertain wait to see how much of the money he says he is owed will ever arrive.

But despite the legal battles, poor communication and the collapse of the league, Herbert isn’t backing away from his original decision.

“I’m still very happy with the decision I made,” Herbert said. “It doesn’t look like I’m in a great position right now, but time will tell.”

Tim Schmitt is the managing editor of Golfweek.

title: World Tennis CEO Ross Hutchins open to keeping Davis Cup Final 8 in Bologna long term
article_text:
- Hutchins said the temptation to keep the Davis Cup Final 8 in Bologna for as long as possible is strong.

- A three-year contract with Angelo Binaghi's Italian federation means the 2027 Final 8 will also be in Italy.

- World Tennis launched a multi-year partnership with Generali, already Davis Cup presenting sponsor, to grow tennis globally.

World Tennis CEO Ross Hutchins has said there is a strong temptation to keep the Davis Cup Final 8 in Bologna for as many years as possible, praising the venue and the Italian tennis federation. World Tennis is the new name of the ITF, which holds the rights to the competition.

"When we have a venue like this, the temptation to stay for as many years as possible is very strong," Hutchins said. He added that the organisers believe they have a high-quality product in Bologna but must also take into account the many nations around the world that take part in the event, and that a balance must be found. He said the current format is a winning one and that a solution for the future can be discussed, because what is being done is working very well.

- Free on iPhone and Android · rated 4.4 on the App Store

For now, a three-year contract signed with the Italian federation led by Angelo Binaghi means the 2027 Final 8 will also be played in Italy, leaving room for a further extension of the collaboration.

Hutchins also said the Davis Cup has found the best possible formula, with home and away ties in the preliminary rounds and a final stage featuring the best eight teams. "The Davis Cup, with its history and the passion it stirs in every country, is something special," he said, adding that the best players compete in the best venues with the best television coverage and partners. He said the current model, running from February to September with home and away ties and then a final phase in November, works very well.

Meanwhile, World Tennis has launched a wide-ranging multi-year partnership with the Italian insurance giant Generali, which was already the presenting sponsor of the Davis Cup. Significant investments will be made to accelerate the global growth of tennis and bring as many people as possible closer to the sport.

"There is a strong correlation between playing tennis and longevity. I still play tennis myself," joked Philippe Donnet, CEO of the Generali group, who said the partnership fits the company's Lifetime Partner strategy and its belief that more active and connected people lead healthier, happier and more fulfilling lives.

The programme includes increasing the number of Masters Tour tournaments and players by 10% in 2027; the tour currently involves more than 42,000 athletes aged between 30 and 100, competing in more than 650 tournaments in 75 countries. It also aims to support the Junior Tennis Initiative with the goal of introducing tennis to more than one million young people each year, and to help World Tennis reach its stated aim of adding 20 million practitioners by 2035. The partnership also covers support for coach training programmes, a fund for new facilities and national training centres, and investment in mass-participation initiatives around Davis Cup matches; between 25,000 and 40,000 children are attending this week's Final 8 matches in Bologna.

Based on the original report by La Gazzetta dello Sport: Hutchins (World Tennis): “Davis a Bologna? La tentazione è di restarci a lungo”

title: OKX continues as McLaren Racing’s primary partner through new three-year deal
article_text:
OKX has extended its partnership with McLaren Racing for a further three years, strengthening a commercial relationship that has grown into one of the most prominent collaborations between a cryptocurrency exchange and a Formula 1 team.

The renewal will see OKX continue as a primary partner of the British outfit, maintaining an association that began in 2022.

Since the initial agreement, the partnership has evolved beyond conventional branding rights, with both organisations developing campaigns that combine motorsport heritage, digital innovation and fan engagement. OKX branding has featured prominently across McLaren’s Formula 1 operations, while the collaboration has also delivered several high-profile activations at selected Grand Prix weekends.

Among the notable initiatives was the introduction of the Stealth Mode livery for the 2023 Singapore and Japanese Grands Prix. The following year, the partnership produced a special Ayrton Senna-inspired livery for the Monaco Grand Prix, paying tribute to the Brazilian driver’s legacy. It also introduced Race Rewind, a digital collectibles initiative designed to offer fans exclusive rewards and experiences.

The collaboration continued in 2025 with a Riviera-inspired livery for the Monaco Grand Prix, drawing inspiration from McLaren’s motorsport history.

The three-year extension underlines both organisations’ intention to build on these initiatives and further explore opportunities across technology, digital engagement and global fan experiences. For OKX, the partnership provides continued access to Formula 1’s international audience, while McLaren benefits from the continuity of an established commercial relationship.

Neither organisation has disclosed the financial terms of the renewed agreement or outlined any changes to the sponsorship rights and activation commitments.

The renewal further highlights the importance of long-term commercial partnerships in Formula 1, where brands are increasingly looking beyond traditional sponsorship visibility to develop deeper connections with fans through content, technology and experiential marketing.

McLaren heads into the final two rounds of the 2026 Formula 1 season occupying fourth position in the Constructors’ Championship with 431 points. Lando Norris sits fifth in the Drivers’ Championship with 264 points, while Oscar Piastri is seventh with 167. Norris secured victory at the Brazilian Grand Prix and finished second in Las Vegas, with Piastri joining him on the podium in third at the latter event. The team will next compete at the Qatar Grand Prix from November 27–29, before concluding its campaign at the Abu Dhabi Grand Prix from December 4–6.

title: Canal+ secures Broadcast rights for Inaugural Icons Cup South Afri
article_text:
Multi-territory agreement with CANAL+ and the ICONS Series – a global golf competition featuring sporting icons from multiple disciplines – brings the inaugural ICONS Cup South Africa to audiences across Sub-Saharan Africa and France, as well as selected international territories, reinforcing CANAL+’s premium sports offering across Africa.

- SuperSport to deliver live coverage of the inaugural ICONS Cup South Africa to Sub-Saharan Africa from The Links at Fancourt, George, from 11-13 December, 2026, on SuperSport Grandstand Africa DStv Channel 221 and on SuperSport Golf Africa DStv Channel 233.

- Comprehensive rights package includes live world feed coverage, opening and closing ceremonies, additional programming, and highlights.

South Africa, 11 November 2026: Global media and entertainment company CANAL+ has acquired the broadcast rights to the ICONS Cup South Africa across Sub-Saharan Africa, France and selected international territories. The event will take place at The Links at Fancourt, George, from 11–13 December 2026.

ICONS Cup, part of the ICONS Series, is a world-first disruptive experiential sports and entertainment brand that brings together the biggest and boldest cross-section of world-class athletes in a competitive golf arena. By uniting some of the world’s most recognisable sporting personalities in a match play golf showdown, the series continues to reimagine the intersection of professional sport and live entertainment.

For ICONS Cup South Africa, Africa’s leading sports broadcaster, SuperSport, will bring the tournament live to audiences across DStv subscribers, with morning sessions airing on SuperSport Grandstand Africa DStv Channel 221 and on SuperSport Golf Africa DStv Channel 233.

The three-day tournament will see two teams, Team South Africa and Team World, go head-to-head, as sporting icons from rugby, cricket, football, golf, swimming and tennis swap their respective sporting arenas for the fairways in one of the most unique sporting crossover events.

Four-time Major champion Ernie Els will captain South Africa, while two-time Masters champion José María Olazábalwill lead Team World, with a stellar ensemble of player announcements to follow. Through SuperSport’s extensive reach, the competition will be available to audiences across Sub-Saharan Africa.

Production will be delivered by ICONS Series, combining premium golf coverage with entertainment-led storytelling and enhanced access to players throughout the competition.

Chris Sice, Chief Content Officer, ICONS Series, said: “Our ambition with ICONS Series has always been to break traditional broadcast moulds and bring audiences closer to the drama than ever before. Partnering with a global powerhouse like Canal+, alongside SuperSport’s unmatched pedigree across Sub-Saharan Africa, marks a major milestone as we bring the Icons Series to South Africa. By pairing premium golf coverage with entertainment-led storytelling, mic’d-up access, and high-tempo match-play, we’re delivering a fast-paced, lean-forward live show that is as fiercely competitive as it is entertaining.”

Rendani Ramovha, CANAL+ Senior Vice-President for Sports Content in English- and Portuguese-speaking Africa, said: “We are delighted to bring the inaugural ICONS Cup South Africa to audiences across Sub-Saharan Africa. Through CANAL+’s global partnerships, we continue to deliver premium sporting events and world-class entertainment to our subscribers. We look forward to showcasing this exciting new competition from Fancourt through SuperSport.”

Audiences can follow the action live on SuperSport Grandstand Africa DStv Channel 221 and on SuperSport Golf Africa DStv Channel 233, with additional coverage and highlights available on SuperSport Blitz DStv Channel 220 AND DStv CatchUp.

For more information, visit www.icons-series.com or visit supersport.com.

title: Tickford Racing strikes significant sponsorship extension
article_text:
Castrol considered its relationship with Tickford among its most successful with 92 race wins and is the second in its motorsport sponsorship portfolio alongside M-Sport.

Castrol first partnered with the Supercars heavyweights in 2003 under the Ford Performance Racing banner, through the Prodrive period and into the Tickford era.

‍”We’re thrilled to announce the extension of the Castrol-Tickford partnership into Year 25 and beyond,” said Castrol Australia and New Zealand head of marketing Jotika Prasad.

“Castrol’s commitment to Australian motorsport is a vital part of our DNA, and Castrol’s partnership with Tickford is certainly a key element of that.

“Castrol’s global association with Ford and Ford Racing programs is something we’re very proud of, and it’s certainly special that one of our longest-standing motorsport associations is right here in Australia.”

Tickford Racing will go into 2027 with an unchanged driver line-up of Cameron Waters and Thomas Randle.

Since graduating from the Super2 Series to Supercars, Randle has carried Castrol’s colours on his cars.

“It’s fantastic to announce that Castrol has re-signed with Tickford Racing for 2027 and beyond,” Randle said.

“I’m super pumped to continue our amazing partnership, a deal that has been going for 25 years.

“It just shows incredible loyalty between Tickford Racing and Castrol and I know that it’s a partnership that is valued.

“Castrol has been my number one supporter for many years now – not only in Supercars but also through my junior ranks.

“We’ve done some amazing things together, whether at the track or off it, I just can’t wait to see what’s in store for 2027 and beyond.”

Tickford Racing chief executive officer Simon Brookhouse hailed the long-standing relationship between his team and Castrol.

‍”We are incredibly proud to continue our longstanding partnership with Castrol,” said Brookhouse.‍

“The Castrol brand is integral to who we are as a race team and without their loyal support we would not be in the position we are in today.

“Castrol’s support and passion for what we do is amazing and it allows us to continue to push boundaries within the race team.

“It goes without saying, but to be one of Castrol’s longest standing partnerships globally is something we do not take for granted and we are excited to continue with them into the future.”

title: Louis Rees-Zammit stood down from Wales squad with immediate effect
article_text:
Louis Rees-Zammit has been ruled out of Wales' clash with Japan at Allianz Stadium, with the winger withdrawn just over an hour before kick-off due to illness.

Wales have confirmed that Ellis Mee will take his place in the starting XV, while Tom Rogers has been brought onto the bench.

Despite claiming a historic victory over the All Blacks this autumn, Wales finished fifth in the northern hemisphere standings.

They will now face Japan in London, with ninth place in the overall Nations Championship table up for grabs.

Rees-Zammit had been expected to play a key role once again, having started all three of Wales' autumn fixtures.

The 25-year-old scored against both Japan and New Zealand, helping his side secure a memorable victory over the All Blacks at the Principality Stadium.

He was unable to find the scoresheet against Australia in last week's defeat and will now miss the return meeting with Japan.

The withdrawal comes during an important period in Rees-Zammit's rugby comeback. After leaving Gloucester in January 2024, he spent 18 months attempting to make it in the NFL.

The winger joined the NFL's International Player Pathway Programme before signing with the Kansas City Chiefs and later the Jacksonville Jaguars.

However, he failed to secure a place on a 53-man roster and ultimately decided to return to rugby.

He joined Bristol Bears ahead of the 2025/26 campaign and made an immediate impression, scoring on his Premiership debut against Leicester Tigers.

Rees-Zammit first rose to prominence at Gloucester, becoming the youngest player to feature in the Premiership at just 18 years old.

His performances earned him 14 Wales caps, with the winger scoring 14 international tries.

He was also part of Wales' 2021 Six Nations-winning squad before representing the British and Irish Lions on their tour of South Africa later that year, scoring three tries in four appearances.

He was subsequently selected for Wales' 2026 Six Nations and Nations Championship squads, continuing his return to international rugby.

title: England were fined by World Rugby for haka response that crossed the line
article_text:
England will have another opportunity to face down the New Zealand haka today – seven years after their controversial response to the All Blacks' pre-match ritual landed them with a £2,000 fine.

Steve Borthwick's side meet New Zealand with the haka once again likely to provide one of the most eagerly anticipated moments before kick-off.

There was a reminder of England's history of confronting the famous Maori challenge last week, when former captain Lewis Moody joined the players on the pitch to face the All Blacks' traditional performance.

Moody, who was diagnosed with motor neurone disease last year, walked out alongside current skipper Maro Itoje before taking his place at the front of England's formation. It was an emotional moment, with the 2003 World Cup winner receiving a huge ovation before being embraced by the current players.

But England's history of confronting the All Blacks' ritual stretches back much further, with their V-shaped response in the 2019 Rugby World Cup semi-final proving particularly controversial.

As is customary, New Zealand performed the haka before their meeting with England in Yokohama, but Eddie Jones' team had no intention of simply standing in a straight line and watching.

Instead, England arranged themselves in a V formation as the All Blacks advanced towards them, creating one of the defining images of the tournament.

Several players, including Joe Marler, Ben Youngs, Elliot Daly, Billy Vunipola, Luke Cowan-Dickie and Mark Wilson, ended up crossing the halfway line and entering New Zealand's half of the pitch.

That was against World Rugby regulations, which state that the team receiving the cultural challenge must remain within its own half.

Referee Nigel Owens and his officials were forced to intervene, ushering several England players back behind the halfway line before kick-off.

England were subsequently fined £2,000 by World Rugby for breaching the tournament's rules relating to cultural challenges.

In a statement, the governing body said: "England have been fined for a breach of Rugby World Cup 2019 tournament rules relating to cultural challenges, which states that no players from the team receiving the challenge may advance beyond the halfway line.

"This is in line with the protocol which operates globally across the international game and is adopted by major international tournaments."

The punishment did little to dampen England's enthusiasm for their approach, with Jones' side going on to produce one of the finest performances in their history by beating the All Blacks 19-7 to reach the World Cup final.

Captain Owen Farrell explained afterwards that his team had wanted to make a statement with their positioning.

"We didn't just want to stand in a flat line and let them come at us," he said.

Manu Tuilagi subsequently revealed that it was Jones who had suggested the unusual formation.

"Everyone wanted to show that we were ready and together. It was something different that I think Eddie suggested," he said.

title: "£1,700 problem" - Andy Farrell takes aim at rugby bosses as 50,000 seats left empty at Twickenham
article_text:
Andy Farrell has questioned the Nations Championship finals weekend format after Ireland beat Australia 38-14 in front of thousands of empty seats at Twickenham.

Around 32,000 tickets were reportedly sold for Friday’s double-header, leaving 50,000 seats empty at the home of English rugby.

The entire upper tier of the stadium was closed.

Farrell was quick to point out that Ireland would have played in front of a packed stadium had the fixture been held in Dublin.

One of the biggest problems with the new competition is that supporters have less than a week to arrange their travel once the finals weekend fixtures are confirmed.

Farrell highlighted that flights from Ireland had reached £1,700.

“If we’d played at the Aviva [in Dublin] it would have been full tonight,” Farrell said, as quoted by The Guardian.

The Ireland boss remains a fan of the competition but was disappointed that more supporters were unable to make the trip.

Adult tickets for Friday’s double-header started at £60, according to The Irish Times.

Throw in flights, a hotel and a couple of days in London, and it’s easy to see why many supporters stayed at home.

England’s clash with the All Blacks on Saturday should attract a much bigger crowd, while France and South Africa will contest the final on Sunday.

There is clearly work to be done before the next edition of the competition in 2028.

As for Ireland, Farrell’s men could hardly have asked for a better November.

🗣️ 'I don't know whether the Friday night thing works...'

🗣️ 'If we'd have played at the Aviva, it would have been full tonight!'

Andy Farrell offers his thoughts on the #NationsChampionship finals weekend format. | 🏉

title: RFU chief Bill Sweeney makes thoughts clear after Andy Farrell criticism
article_text:
RFU chief executive Bill Sweeney has defended the Nations Championship finals weekend, insisting the inaugural competition has been a success despite criticism from Ireland head coach Andy Farrell.

Around 50,000 seats were left empty at the home of English rugby, with the entire upper tier closed.

Farrell suggested the fixture would have attracted a full house at Dublin's Aviva Stadium and also raised concerns over the cost of travelling to London, with flights reportedly reaching £1,700.

Although the Ireland boss remains supportive of the competition, he questioned whether Friday night fixtures were the right approach. His side's victory also completed a perfect November campaign, with four wins from four.

Sweeney has now offered his own assessment of the tournament in an interview with ITV Rugby.

While he did not directly address Farrell's comments, the RFU chief was keen to highlight the overall success of the event and its commercial potential.

"We knew Friday was going to be a tough sell. We has just over 30 [thousand] here last night, but when you consider we've sold 160,000 tickets over three days, where a lot of it is pretty blind, we're really pleased with that.

"If you look at TV viewership, we should get over 100 million people watching it, so that's 170% up from last autumn. We're really happy.

"It's because we were talking to commercial partners and broadcasters, and summer tours are great and autumn internationals are great, but they didn't have enough meaning in them.

"There was a sense of if we can bring those two together, create a meaningful tournament, north vs south, an overall winner, and we thought that would bring more excitement to the fans and make it more commercially viable.

"I think we've seen that and the reaction we've had, all the fans I've spoken to have really liked the format."

Sweeney also made it clear that he believes the competition has a long-term future, although some adjustments could be required.

"It's a tournament that's here to stay, there's probably a few tweaks to be made."

title: Nigel Owens hits out at Rassie Erasmus over six-match ban
article_text:
Nigel Owens has had his say on Rassie Erasmus’ six-match ban ahead of the Springboks’ Nations Championship final against France.

The South Africa boss was banned following comments he made about match officials in the wake of his side’s defeat to France earlier this month.

Writing in his WalesOnline column, Owens pulled no punches.

“He didn’t accuse officials of match-fixing, but he certainly put that question out there.

“Of course, he has a history of doing this - as we all know.”

The Welshman, who revealed he received homophobic abuse and death threats during his own refereeing career, believes comments like those made by Erasmus only make matters worse.

“All this does is heighten the pressure on referees - and with that comes abuse.”

However, Owens is not convinced rugby has got everything right when it comes to coaches raising concerns about officials.

He questioned the apparent five-clip limit on incidents coaches can submit for review, recalling his dealings with former Ireland boss Joe Schmidt.

“When I was reffing Ireland, Joe Schmidt would be sending in 45 clips to look at if they lost!

“Do coaches have a point when they question officials? Of course they do.”

Despite that, Owens believes Erasmus will eventually regret his choice of words.

“I’m sure, when he reflects on it, he’ll realise he went about it the wrong way.”

Owens has also given his verdict on the decision to issue Dan Sheehan with a retrospective red card and suspension following his dangerous crocodile roll on Marco van Staden last week.

The Ireland captain was handed a two-week ban after his red card during Ireland's 20-17 victory over South Africa in Dublin.

The hooker was initially sent to the sin bin for a dangerous crocodile roll on Springboks flanker Marco van Staden, with his yellow card subsequently upgraded to red.

An independent disciplinary committee upheld the decision, ruling that Sheehan had breached Law 9.20d.

The two-week suspension was deemed appropriate due to the low entry point of the offence, with Sheehan accepting the sanction.

He will miss Ireland's clash with Australia, as well as Leinster's URC fixture against Ospreys.

Speaking on the latest edition of World Rugby's Whistle Watch, legendary referee Owens backed the decision and explained why both incidents during the match had reached the red card threshold.

“You have got the croc roll, you have got that dangerous action. He [Sheehan] twists the body, and then he goes down and there is pressure on that lower limb which is dangerous.

“So, they would have reached that (red card) threshold, and then the clear-out as well, you have got head contact they deemed to be reckless and then that would reach a threshold as well.

“Now what happens here is the time of the game came to an end, so they [the Foul Play Review Officer] didn’t get back to the referee. This now is upgraded to a red for both players and they stay off.

“But what would happen then is the foul play review officer after the game would say, well, look, this has reached the red card threshold.

"Obviously there is a judicial process in place by the Nations Championship; they are responsible for that, and obviously the judicial process here has given a two-game ban for the croc roll (and three for the clear-out).

“So that is how the referees would have looked. Both were foul play; they both reached the threshold of dangerous play, and so you need to judge as a referee which one of those two you felt was the most dangerous.

“Or if both are the same for you, then I would assume you probably restart with the first one, which should have been a penalty to South Africa (it was and they kicked to touch).

"But definitely the outcome, [it is the] correct yellow card threshold and I would say yeah, probably reached the red card threshold.”

Owens also discussed the decision to clear Ireland fly-half Sam Prendergast following his citing against Fiji.

The 23-year-old appeared before an independent Disciplinary Committee last Tuesday after being cited for an alleged breach of Law 9.13, which relates to dangerous tackling.

The decision allowed him to face the Springboks last weekend, providing Andy Farrell with a timely boost ahead of the heavyweight encounter.

“Basically, what has happened is they didn’t feel that it reached the red card threshold.

“Yes, you have got that grasp, you have got the swings, it is a drop tackle.

“But when it got then to the judicial to look at it, they decided, well, look, no, we don’t think that this reaches the red card threshold.

"It is a clear example of what a drop tackle is, just that it wasn’t a red card offence, hence why they said he [Prendergast] is fine to play.”

- Born on 18 June 1971 in Carmarthenshire, Wales.

- Made his international refereeing debut in 2003.

- Became the first referee to officiate 100 Test matches.

- Refereed the 2015 Rugby World Cup final between New Zealand and Australia.

- Officiated at four consecutive Rugby World Cups.

- Named World Rugby Referee of the Year in 2015.

- Issued just three red cards and 59 yellow cards across 100 Tests.

- Retired from international refereeing in December 2020.

- Remains involved in rugby as a pundit and refereeing expert.

- Awarded an honorary doctorate by the University of Bath in 2024.

title: Alcaraz, Spain through to Davis Cup final after win over Britain
article_text:
BOLOGNA, Italy — Carlos Alcaraz powered Spain past Britain on Saturday and into the Davis Cup final, earning a title rematch with Italy.

Six-time champion Spain beat Britain 2-0 in the semifinals in Bologna, Alcaraz clinching victory with a straight sets-win against Arthur Fery.

Alcaraz completed a career Grand Slam this season and bounced back from a wrist injury that sidelined him for nearly five months by winning the ATP Finals last week.

On Sunday, the 23-year-old Spaniard can add a Davis Cup title to his superb season if he can help his team beat Italy, which is without injured world No. 2 Jannik Sinner.

“I’m just really happy, really proud, giving that point to qualify Spain for the final,” Alcaraz said. “It’s the second straight final for us, and my first Davis Cup final. I’m going to do whatever it takes to win."

The No. 3-ranked Alcaraz swept aside Fery, who stunned tennis with his unlikely run to the Wimbledon semifinals this year, 6-2, 6-1.

Fery had the daunting task of having to beat Alcaraz to take the tie to a doubles decider after Rafael Jodar overcame Cameron Norrie 6-2, 7-5.

Alcaraz has had fitness issues in recent weeks and didn't play in Spain's quarterfinal against Austria on Thursday. But he was back in action on Saturday, needing only 72 minutes to wrap up the win.

Italy has won the tournament for three consecutive years, including a 2-0 victory over a Spain side missing Alcaraz in last season's final.

Spain is aiming to win the competition for the first time since 2019.

On Friday, Italy booked its spot in the final after Lorenzo Musetti and Andrea Vavassori won the deciding doubles to clinch a 2-1 win over Czechia.

title: Musetti pulls off double duty, Italy claws into fourth straight Davis Cup final
Sinner won't play 1st Grand Slam tennis tournament of 2027
article_text:
Jannik Sinner won't compete in the first Grand Slam tennis tournament of 2027 while he recovers from recent right knee surgery, Australian Open officials said Thursday.

"We've been in regular touch with Jannik's team and they've confirmed he won't be joining us for the AO in January following his recent surgery," Tennis Australia chief executive Andrew Abdo said in a statement to The Associated Press.

"Jannik loves competing here in Melbourne and is looking forward to returning for AO 2028. We wish him all the very best with his recovery and look forward to seeing him back on court soon."

On Tuesday, Sinner said he had undergone a "minor" operation on his bothersome right knee because it hadn't responded well to other treatments. He didn't give a timeline for his return to the tour.

Sinner hasn't played since defending his Wimbledon title in July for his fifth Grand Slam singles trophy, and he recently lost the No. 1 ranking to Alexander Zverev.

"I have to respect the protocols at the moment because if we rush things we could have more serious problems," Sinner said during a news conference in Milan earlier this month.

When Sinner shut down his 2026 season last month, with a statement from his management team saying the 25-year-old Italian "will follow a course of treatment for inflammation in his knee."

It's the second prolonged absence from the tennis tour in two years after Sinner accepted a three-month ban in a settlement with the World Anti-Doping Agency for a doping case in 2025.
